subsubtopic: INTEREST RATES PAID BY BANKS ON DEPOSITS-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to seek consent of the House to move a motion in a case of urgent and pressing necessity. If it is accepted I have no plans to debate it, and I hope no one else will. The urgent situation concerns the action of the Bank of Montreal, as disclosed to me this morning, of responding immediately to the decision of the
Bank of Canada to increase the interest rate by one percentage point by raising its prime rate from 9'/2 per cent to 10 'A per cent for loans but not yet raising the interest rate payable on deposits for the benefit of its customers. I would therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett):
That this House is of the opinion that chartered banks, at the moment of increasing interest rates on loans, should also increase the interest rates payable to customers for money on deposit with the banks.

subsubtopic: SUPPLY OF RAILWAY BOXCARS IN ATLANTIC PROVINCES- REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to Standing Order 43. In view of the nationwide shortage of rolling stock on our railways and reports that Canadian National Railways has informed the president of Scott Maritimes Pulp Limited and others that a further withdrawal of boxcars will be made from the Atlantic region which, if carried out, in the case of Scott alone will result in a production curtailment and cost in excess of $100,000 per month for alternate shipping arrangements, and which also will affect shippers of fertilizer, peat moss and other staples of the Maritimes economy, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell):
That the Minister of Transport, who indicated recently that it would be improper to take boxcars from the Atlantic area for use in the west because this would hurt the Atlantic economy, take all necessary steps and exert whatever authority he may have left to prevent the Atlantic region from being shortchanged by our national railway system.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of very urgent and pressing necessity, namely, the growing volume of egg imports from the United States, which is destroying the viability of the Canadian egg industry. Due to the recent high volume of imports and the probability of this level drastically increasing, plus the cost to the Canadian Egg Marketing Agency to remove these imports and thereby try to maintain orderly marketing and pricing in Canada, I move, seconded by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens):
That this House instruct the Minister of Agriculture to take immediate steps to counteract the importation of United States eggs into Canada in order to protect the Canadian egg industry from below cost of production United States eggs further destroying our market in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I was interrupted by the clock last evening I had not even had the opportunity to say that I will be supporting the general thrust of this bill. I feel that it is important for me to make a few specific comments about two or three clauses.
First, I, like some of my colleagues, want to destroy the illusion which was created by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) in some literature he had printed and distributed in connection with the presentation of this bill. A claim was made in that literature that one of the major purposes of this bill was the elimination of discrimination between the sexes.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
As I was saying, the Minister of National Health and Welfare was willing to
April 18, 1974

leave the impression that one purpose of this bill was the elimination of discrimination on the basis of sex. One clause purports to do this. However, it would be most improper if the country were misled in this regard. I agree with those who have said that this is an entirely misleading representation. No doubt other members will make the same statement. Nevertheless, a step in the right direction has been taken. It is worthwhile and I am glad it has been taken. Let us not fool ourselves, let us not fool the nation. This provision does not finally eliminate discrimination between the sexes on the basis of pensions paid under the Canada Pension Plan. For example, housewives are not reckoned with here. They are not permitted to contribute and they are not allowed to apply in their own right for these pension privileges.
This bill merely adopts a principle that would allow others to cover you with virtue, especially when your own virtue is tarnished. However, I am forced to admit that the amendment to clause 56, which appears on page 25, provides for an upward adjustment of the pension due to the surviving spouse. There are two elements in this particular clause which I welcome, one the upward adjustment from 50 to 60 per cent and, two, the provision for the surviving spouse. In other words, there is no specific mention of the widow or the widower, but the one who survives. However, I do not consider the proportion sufficiently great. Like my colleague, the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), I think 60 per cent is a pretty low rating for a surviving spouse of whatever sex. If we have to set the amount in percentage terms, and I suppose in the long run we must do that, I think 75 or 80 per cent would be nearer the mark.
I am very heartened to see this principle adopted because I am reminded of some remarks I made in this House on March 11 in my contribution to the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. At that time I argued that it is grossly unfair to expect the surviving member of a couple to carry on with only 50 per cent of the revenue from the old age pensions that were enjoyed when the two were living. There are many continuing expenses. It is not just a matter of half the number of people. The roof still has to be maintained, the telephone paid and the gutter around the roof may have to be replaced. A surviving spouse has to deal with many things. Furthermore, the surviving spouse is not always able, at the age the pension is due, to do work himself or herself and must employ casual labour, if he or she can afford it at the reduced revenue. I say we have further to go in this direction.
I am not entirely sure I understand the full financial implications or impact of 56(1)(a)(i) where an amount of 37Vi per cent is introduced. I hope the minister or the parliamentary secretary will elucidate further on that.
My next comment concerns the means test. I am glad to see it has been eliminated. Insofar as it is determined on the basis of age, it has had some pretty strange results. For example, when a friend of mine reached the age of 65, he was sent a form to complete in order to qualify for the Canada Pension Plan. He filled it in, submitted it and in due course, fairly promptly, the pension began to arrive regularly. When he filled out his income tax return at the
Canada Pension Plan
end of the year, he received a very rude shock. He entered this revenue on his tax return and paid the tax on it. After the income tax return was received by the Income Tax Department, he received a letter from the pension people stating that he should not have been receiving the pension because his earnings were greater than those that merited the payment of the Canada Pension Plan at that age and that he must repay the pension. Happily, because of revenues he enjoyed during that year, he was able to make that repayment. It was not pleasant, but he did it.
Things went smoothly for this person for the next two or three years. After he passed his 69th birthday, he received another form. He had heard talk about a gradual reduction in the age of eligibility for the Canada Pension Plan from age 70 to 69 to 68, so he again filled in a form. The payments resumed. After filling in his income tax return this year, he has once again been told that he must repay those payments to the Canada Pension Plan. He did that, but perhaps not quite so easily. For a variety of reasons, his revenue on the earlier occasion was better than in the last year and therefore he was rudely shocked when told he would have to repay, without the appropriate adjustment in income tax I am led to believe, that portion of his income which came from the Canada Pension Plan. Therefore, I am glad that part of the problem is being eliminated by amendments that are now before us.
I have other concerns about the means test. I have had these for a long time. Here I will be speaking for myself and not for anyone else in my party. I want to make it clear that I think a means test of some kind is desirable. It should not be on the basis of age, but rather on the basis of income and income alone. There are some who do not need the Canada Pension Plan payments. There are some who work and put away money to look after their own future and the future of their family. I am glad of that. That virtue should be cultivated. We should certainly not discourage it. I do not disagree one bit with the cradle to the grave notion for those in need, and here I swiftly interject for those in need. Otherwise, I maintain we are destroying a very fundamental virtue in man, his sense of responsibility, resourcefulness and concern to look after himself and his family in his own way without leaning on the government or anyone else.
Governments have not always been considerate, let us remind ourselves, in human terms, as we can see even from the events of the last few weeks. Can anyone rely on government to be paternal when the time comes? If you are in need, you have no option, but when you are not in need I think you should not be obliged to accept this pension. In my view, a man should be encouraged by every means to look after himself and his family in his own way.
Having said this, I recognize that everyone is not able to do so, unfortunately. There are some who, through circumstances beyond their control, are not able to provide for themselves and their families. They may work all their lives and yet be unable to save for a rainy day. Let them save through the Canada Pension Plan. Why not? To this extent I favour the plan, but I think it should be regarded as a fail-back position, not as a primary post on which to lean.

April 18, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
Speaking to this bill on second reading, as reported in Hansard on page 1482, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) talked about families drawing $700 a month under the Canada Pension Plan and OAS allowances in 1985. This is a figure I find staggering. Have we paused to calculate what it would mean in terms of dollars from the treasury-what it would mean in terms of taxation? I am deeply concerned at the prospect. For those in need, fine. They will need every penny of that $700, the way things are going, unless there is a drastic change in the next month or so. But this should only be a backstop for those who have not been discouraged from looking ahead and providing for their own needs. Consider the extra burden that $700 a month would mean in terms of income tax-another $8,400 a year on which to pay tax. I suggest indeed, that payments should not be made even by way of AOS benefits-and here I know I am being heretical-unless requested. In this way we might avoid the difficulty referred to by my hon. friend and also the problem of the unnecessary income tax. The OAS payments and the Canada Pension Plan payments might be allowed to accumulate as savings, as a savings account, if you will, until such time as someone is in need, with the proviso that in case of a sudden demise the savings which have been accumulated pass into the estate of the deceased.
I must say I am not really happy about the amendment proposed to section 63(1) of the act related to the determination of the legal identity of the surviving spouse. The seven year "living together" principle has been dropped and in its place a three year period has been inserted.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: What about common-law?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Common-law people are pretty well looked after, I gather. I am talking about legally married couples. The time requirement in the amendment on page 25 has been reduced to nil. The surviving spouse of a deceased contributor is defined as the person who was by law married to the deceased contributor at the time of his death. I suggest that this is open to abuse and I should like to see a change made in committee.
With these comments, I close my reflections on the bill before us. However, I should like to summarize. First, I definitely reject the notion which the government has allowed to grow up that discrimination on the basis of sex has been eliminated by the bill before us. Second, I favour a means test and a deferment program for CPP and OAS, both of which should be optional. Finally, I am unhappy about the definition of a surviving spouse as "the person who was by law married to the deceased contributor at the time of his death." I think I should like to see a two or three year element introduced here to avoid abuses of or by, let us say, sugar daddies.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on Bill C-19 I must say to the House that I was not here when the bill was first introduced or when second reading began. However, I have read the speeches which have been made. I took particular note of the speech made by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie). At the beginning of his remarks, he said:
Mr. Speaker, I begin by giving the minister a hint that this measure will pass.

That was a pretty brave thing to do, because a similar bill was presented to the previous parliament and I was successful in making certain that it did not pass. There is a significant difference between the bill before us now and the bill which was presented to the previous parliament. I should like to warn the minister and the hon. member for Hillsborough that the most significant difference I could find between the two bills was that the previous one contained seven clauses and the present bill contains 57. I have had some experience with regard to the passing, or failure to pass, of legislation brought before the House of Commons. I would remind all hon. members, particularly new members, that it is very difficult to block a bill which is only seven clauses long. Sometimes one is successful, sometimes not. Last session, I and a few others were successful.
I have counted the pages of Bill C-19, and I find there are 46. Now, there are a lot of words in 46 pages, and under our rules one can move to amend virtually every one of them. Mr. Speaker, you are an able person in your job, and you can group those amendments for debate in any way you please. Nevertheless, I believe the hon. member for Hillsborough, when he gave the minister a hint that this measure would pass, was a very brave person because I do not give the minister that hint. I would be less than honest with this House if I made anyone believe that I will contribute in any way to the passage of this legislation, because I will not. I think it is a mistake. It is poor legislation and I will do my best to encourage all members not to assist in its passage and to oppose it in every way.
I say to the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) and other members of the House that there will be votes, and I address my remarks particularly to members from Alberta. Their votes with regard to exempting various religious groups from this particular tax that the government has placed on all Canadians, a tax that this legislation is now increasing will be noted by Albertans.
Having made very clear to all members my stated intentions in the debate on this bill, I will now attempt to explain why I am so firm in my dedication to block this measure. First of all, the Canada Pension Plan covers only one third of the population of Canada. My hon. friends to my left, of whom there happens to be none here today, are forever talking about rip-offs and windfalls. When the Canada Pension Plan was first passed in 1966 there was a windfall age group, and, "windfall," became quite a common term. The first time I ever heard the word was in this House of Commons in 1966. This windfall age group fell between the ages of 55 and 65, people who were eligible for the Canada Pension Plan. This group of people were designated a windfall age group because they were going to get more from the Canada Pension Plan than they paid into it.
According to a report I read in a Toronto newspaper, though I do not have it here with me, the leader of the New Democratic Party is in this windfall age group. The first year he becomes eligible for the CPP at 65 he is going to receive more money from the plan than he has paid into it during the previous ten years. I am not going to suggest that the hon. member is going to accept a rip-off; he is against rip-offs and very often speaks in this House in
April 18, 1974

disparaging tones about them, so I do not think he would accept one. But I merely point out, to make it firm and clear in everyone's minds, that there is a windfall group that will reap more from the Canada Pension Plan than they put into it. I notice one member of the NDP is now here and he can correct me if anything I have said during the last few minutes is absolutely wrong.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if there is a windfall group, then there is also a group of people who are going to pay more into the plan than they can possibly reap; that stands to reason. If there is a windfall group on one side of the ledger, there must be another group on the other side. Who comprise this group on the other side? Basically these are the 18 year olds who are entering the labour force today, or tomorrow or yesterday for that matter. They are the 16 year olds even, if they enter the labour force at that age. They will pay, for easy mathematics, for 50 years into the CPP, and pay into it far more than they will take out, provided the longevity of the average Canadian is not extended far beyond what it is today.
As I have said, only one third of the population is covered by the Canada Pension Plan. This piece of legislation is exempting another two groups. I am not going to go on at length about whether or not they are good Canadian citizens. I made a speech on the CPP bill in the last session, I think it was Bill C-190, and I was quoted as saying that Hutterites are not good Canadian citizens. I was quoting a brief, a study carried out by and for the Alberta government, in which the commissioners stated that they were not good Canadian citizens. I remember the debate we had on that bill very well. Some members of parliament broadcast across the air waves of western Canada their opinion that they were the best citizens, honourable Canadians, but I am not going to get into that. Each member of this House and Your Honour can determine in his or her mind what makes a good citizen.
Legislation has been presented to the House from time to time which singles out a specific group of people for special treatment because they are extraordinary citizens-for example the veterans. Our veterans have served Canada, and Canadian parliaments in years gone by-and I suppose parliaments to come will do the same-have brought down specific pieces of legislation for our veterans, who risked their lives to defend what we cherish most, freedom-freedom of the world, freedom of the western world, thus ensuring freedom within Canada. This signifies to me that it is a group needing special mention, that it is a group that has proven its preparedness to serve Canada.
I am not going to tell this House of Commons that all Mennonites are one, that they are all alike, because they are not. Members of the House who are knowledgeable in this regard know of what I speak. The Mennonites referred to in this bill are part of a sect resident in what might be called the southern part of Ontario. They in no way have anything to do with the Mennonites in western Canada; I make that abundantly clear.
This aspect was studied when we were debating Bill C-190 in committee, and at that time the minister informed the committee there had been no application by the Mennonites of western Canada for exemption from the CPP. In fact, the minister stated to the committee-I want
Canada Pension Plan
to make this abundantly clear before the hon. member for Hillsborough leaves, since he made mention of Mennonites who were practising their religion and trying to promote it outside of Canada-that many Mennonites presently living outside Canada had informed the Department of National Health and Welfare that they hoped they could continue to make payments to the Canada Pension Plan because they wanted to look forward to retirement in Canada, a retirement during which they would receive benefits from the Canada Pension Plan. These people are Mennonite missionaries abroad in the world, some of them even in Bangladesh.
So, Mr. Speaker, there is no question in my mind that this particular group of people wants to remain within the Canada Pension Plan. I repeat that the Mennonites of western Canada have made no request for exemption from the CPP. This was clearly stated in the committee proceedings last session.
The other main group that is actively and avidly seeking exemption from the Canada Pension Plan is composed of those commonly referred to as the Hutterites, or the Hut-terian sect, which perhaps is a branch of the early Mennonite order. I am not going into the history of the Hutterites. If any member wants to study them and their way of life he should read a book called "All Things Common," by a university professor who lived with the Hutterites in Manitoba, Victor Peters. That is a very interesting book and it is a very interesting religion. I have no axe to grind in respect of their religion as I fully believe they should be allowed to practise any religion they want within Canada, but I do not believe parliament should take it upon itself to say that one man's religion is better than another. I have made it a practice in public life never to ask anybody his religion, as I believe that is a personal belief and it should be retained as such. I have said in this House on a number of occasions that any religion is better than no religion at all. For you atheists in the House, and this is not for your benefit, Mr. Speaker, as I know you are not one of those, I mean just what I say, that any religion is better than no religion at all, but parliament should not rule that one religion is better than another.
One might ask how I determined that Bill C-19 suggests that one religion is better than another. The minister sometime ago in committee said the Hutterites should be exempt because of their religious beliefs and their zealous desire to take care of their elder citizens. He felt that, based on their past record, they did not need the Canada Pension Plan. One of the most deplorable things about our society today is that governments in recent years, and the present government more so than any other in the past, have encouraged Canadians not to save. It does not pay anybody in Canada to save money today. In fact, the way money is depreciating the quicker you can spend it the better off you are. In any event, governments have not encouraged people to save. You cannot take care of your elder relatives unless you do save.
Let us suppose someone has a government annuity of such and such an amount that will pay such and such a premium to a father and mother when they retire. Does that allow those persons to become exempt from the Canada Pension Plan because that is proof that they can

April 18, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
look after themselves in retirement as well as they could if they were receiving benefits of the Canada Pension Plan? I suggest that does not make them exempt, and that is what the minister indicated.
A number of people in this House have made the suggestion that we in the Conservative party must believe in the freedom of religion, that the Canada Pension Plan does, in fact, prevent the Hutterian Brotherhood from practising their religion freely and that this is a contradiction. That is a very interesting concept, and I wonder what another arm of the government thinks about such a concept. I happen to have with me this afternoon a decision handed down by the Federal Court of Canada on September 15, 1973. This is not an old decision but is relatively new, and it is in respect of a case between a number of Hutterian people, as plaintiffs, and Her Majesty the Queen as defendant. This case was in respect of the payment of income tax by these people, and the suggestion was, by counsel for the plaintiff, that no income tax was leviable against them because they were not in receipt of income. Let me read from page 11 of this decision as follows:
-in any event, the income of a member is found to be taxable by reason of the provisions of the Income Tax Act, such provisions are inoperative because they are in conflict with the provisions of the Canadian Bill of Rights-
That was a reference to the position taken by counsel for the plaintiffs. That suggestion was made during the debate on Bill C-190. The suggestion is that because these provisions are in conflict with the Canadian Bill of Rights, specifically Section 1(c), they in effect interfere with the Hutterites' freedom of religion. The plaintiffs argued that because the Income Tax Act interfered with their freedom of religion it should not apply. The argument in this case was presented on September 11, 12 and 13, 1973. The government argued that the provisions of the Income Tax Act did not interfere with their right of freedom of religion, and at page 22 of the same decision we find the following stated:
Since the objects or purposes of each colony are not exclusively religious they cannot be ... "religious orders" within the meaning of Section 27(2) of the act-
That was clearly spelled out in that judgment at page 22 where we find the following statement, which I think is very significant and which I bring to the attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and his parliamentary assistant:
The application of the Income Tax Act in no way imposes any obligation upon the Hutterites to accept income. All that has been done is to enact legislation within the powers of the Parliament of Canada requiring the taxing authorities to tax the income earned by all Canadians including Hutterites.
What does the Canada Pension Plan do? It in no way imposes a tax on the Hutterites or anybody else if they do not make any income. In fact, this bill has a tendency to increase or broaden the terms of exemptions by increasing the amount one can earn without being subject to payments under the Canada Pension Plan. If you do not earn $600 a year you do not have to contribute one penny to the Canada Pension Plan, or that was the way it was, and this bill refers to the $600 amount and makes it 10 per cent on an adjustable scale, so it will go up over the years.
In any event, the Canada Pension Plan in no way obligates the Hutterites to accept income, and in no way

imposes an obligation on them to pay to the Canada Pension Plan if they make less than $600 a year. They must only pay if they make more than that in earnings as individuals.
Let me just deal for a moment with the definition of "individual", and I did this at some length during the debate on Bill C-190 in respect of the whole question of social security. At pages 17 and 18 of this same judgment we find the following statement:
It is clear then that such earnings are the earnings of the members and are properly included as income in reporting their taxable income-
I do not intend to read the whole paragraph, but that in essence determines whether they should be considered as individuals under the Income Tax Act. Certainly, if they have earnings those earnings are taxable.
During the debate on Bill C-190 I read from the writings of a learned author who wrote about Hutterite teachings centuries ago. I believe his name was Rideman. He stated the Hutterites had no objection to and would comply with all taxes imposed by the government. He went on to state that they should render unto Caesar what is Caesar's. I will not read from his writings again, but the point is that contributions to the Canada Pension Plan are in fact taxes levied on any Canadian who earns income over and above a certain amount. If an individual does not have have an income over that amount the Canada Pension Plan does not apply. The question of whether they are allowed to freely practise their religion has been clearly spelled out. Their defence in respect of the application of the Income Tax Act is the same in respect of this plan, that it interferes with their right to freedom of religion. In any event, the court has ruled that the Income Tax Act did not interfere with that right of freedom of religion.
The defendant in that particular case was the Government of Canada. I commend the Government of Canada for taking that position. Here we have the Government of Canada, however, bringing forward a bill called C-19 which these people feel might interfere with their freedom of religion. It does not and will not. Unless they earn income they will not have to pay any attention to it. Here, clearly, the minister is trying to get rid of his workload because it is difficult to tax the Hutterites as individuals in respect of the Canada Pension Plan. They will not accept social security numbers, so the minister is attempting to lighten his load by increasing the load on every taxpayer of Canada.
The question of whether or not the Canada Pension Plan imposes a tax is interesting. One might look at the definition of the word "tax" in the Random House dictionary of the English language. It has this to say:
1.	a sum of money demanded by a government for its support or for specific facilities or services, levied upon incomes, property, sales, etc.
This is a tax levied by the Government of Canada upon the people for a particular service. It goes on to state:
2.	a burdensome charge, obligation, duty, or demand.-v.t.
3.	(of a government) a. to demand a tax from (a person, business, etc.), b. to demand a tax in consideration of the possession or occurrence ...
April 18, 1974

That pretty well spells out what a tax is. I happen to have another dictionary, the Pocket Oxford edition. It states this in respect of the word "tax":
Legally levied contribution to State revenue, levied from or in respect of; whose burden actually falls on those they are levied from ...
That pretty well spells out the essence of what is a tax. It is a demand by the government upon the people whom the government is attempting to govern. This Canada Pension Plan premium is in essence a tax. I shall not suggest at this time whether or not it is a tax that is fairly applied. I think the fact that it covers only one third of the population of Canada suggests that it is not universal. I supported the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher) in respect of his suggestion during the debate on the other bill that wives should be allowed to contribute a portion equal to their husband's contribution so that they could receive a full pension or in the event that there should be a separation within the family the wife would have made a contribution to the Canada Pension Plan.
An amendment of this type would mean that the legislation would cover a great deal more than one third of the people. I think the basic decision which must be made here is whether certain people are to be given the right of exemption from the Canada Pension Plan and not others. If we adopt the idea that some may be exempt because of religious beliefs then why should others not be exempt. My own religious belief is inferior to that of no one in this House. Therefore, I take great exception to the government suggesting that one religion is better than another. As recorded at page 1482 of Hansard, the minister said that because of his belief in freedom and tolerance he believed certain religious groups should be exempt. No one in this House cherishes his freedom more than 1.1 ask the government and the minister whether they really want this bill to be passed. I know the minister is not particularly fussy this week because this is purely a filler so far as the government is concerned. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came back today and it was nice to see him, but he really wanted to be away this week so they are just putting fillers before the House of Commons to test the wind so to speak. At the outset of my speech I indicated how the wind should blow in respect of Bill C-19.
An hon. Member; And we are hearing it.

speechtext: And you are hearing it, yes. This bill contains 57 clauses. That is sufficient number of clauses for some amendments to be moved. Some clauses contain subclauses and there might be two or three amendments filed in respect of a clause by certain members of the House of Commons. The bill contains 46 pages and there are many words contained on each page. This bill is in for a rough ride, but the Minister of National Health and Welfare knows we may be into an election before we even get through second reading of this bill.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: What are you going to do about it?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
What am I going to do about it? If that is the only way I can kill this bill I hope an election comes along, but the bill shall die if I have my way. As recorded at page 1482 of Hansard, the minister stated that becauce he believes in freedom and tolerance he thinks the
Canada Pension Plan
House should accept exemptions in respect of these two religious orders.
Let us take a look at the question of tolerance. Is it tolerance because the minister thinks these organizations are quasicharitable groups? Let us see what the court had to say with regard to the question of charitable groups. At page 9 the judgment states:
The above, then, sets the framework for these appeals. Counsel for the Plaintiffs early in the trial acknowledged that he was not arguing that the colonies were charitable organizations ...
I have known many lawyers who would not discard any point if they thought it would benefit their client, but this lawyer whom these people hired-and they get the best since they have the money because they have not paid income tax for many years-did not attempt to argue that these were charitable organizations.
The judgment states this clearly at page 9. I will read it again:
Counsel for the Plaintiffs early in the trial acknowledged that he was not arguing that the colonies were charitable organizations within the meaning of Section 62(1) (e) of the Income Tax Act. ..
That disposes of that question in a hurry. Their legal counsel did not argue that they were a charitable organization. Why should the minister, out of the bigness of his heart, which he has demonstrated clearly all across Canada recently on a number of issues, ask for tolerance on the part of the House of Commons when the counsel for these people did not argue that they represent a charitable organization. Then, what are they? This is the question. In order to make it abundantly clear I should like to read from the Hutterite Church doctrine or what one might call their charter. It states this:
Each congregation or community of the Church is empowered, inter alia, as follows:
To engage in, and carry on farming, stock raising, milling, and all
branches of these industries; and to manufacture and deal with the
products and by-products of these industries;
To carry on any other business (whether manufacturing or otherwise) which may seem to said congregation or community of the said Church capable of being conveniently carried on in connection with its business or calculated directly or indirectly to enhance the property or rights of the congregation or community;
That particular part of their charter spells out what they are. In essence they engage in the business of farming, stock raising and milling. This is no secret. Everyone in Alberta knows that they carry on an extensive operation in farming, milling and even manufacturing. When I was a young fellow I used to favour their brand of pancake flour. It made good pancakes, and still does. Now, my wife makes the pancake mix herself rather than buying the ready mixed pancake flour. But if you live in Alberta you can buy their pancake flour. The Hutterites in Alberta are in the manufacturing business. They manufacture pancake flour. It has a brand name and I would be doing them a disservice if I did not mention it. It is called Coyote Howling Pancake Flour, or something like that. In any case it has a picture of the coyote howling, and it makes good pancakes.
The Hutterites do not pay their workers compensation nor do they pay minimum wages in that manufacturing firm. Only recently have they paid income tax, that is

April 18, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
after the judgment of a year ago and the last one which I quoted of last September when the income tax department told them that income taxes must be collected from them.
One can reach any conclusion one wants to on this particular issue. This judgment from which I quoted states very clearly at page 10:
Apparently until the year 1960, the colonies paid no income taxes of any kind.
The first court case was fought in 1966 and the final case was in 1970 with regard to one group of Hutterites commonly referred to as Lehrer-Leuts. I am speaking of Dari-us-Leuts rather than Lehrer-Leuts, and they fought this case on their own, as a separate entity. One or two years ago in May the Lehrer-Leuts lost their case, and last September the Darius-Leuts lost theirs before the federal court of Canada. Both cases were fought on the basis of the concept that the income tax levied against these people would, in one way or another, restrict freedom of religion. The courts ruled it did not.
It is interesting that there should be members of parliament coming before the House trying to make the case that this tax will restrict their freedom of religion. In no way will it affect their religion because, in the first instance, they do not make any income so this tax will never be levied; second, if they have really taken the vow of poverty, they do not want to make an income in any case, so they do not have to worry.
The judgment went on to summarize findings in a similar case. It reads:
... in my opinion, applicable in this case with the result that it would seem there is nothing to preclude the application of the Income Tax Act to the farm income merely because of the reference in each colony's Articles of Association to the promotion of religion.
Before I was led astray I read out the article of the charter of the Hutterites which specifically encourages them to engage in a business. The judge singled out this aspect in particular. I maintain that that particular aspect applies equally to the Canada Pension Plan which in essence is a tax, as I showed by quoting from the two dictionaries earlier. The judgment goes on to say:
... the revenues earned by the Plaintiffs herein are mere depositories for the income earned by each member. Since no distinction can be drawn between individual members each is the recipient of an equal share of the net income, even though it is not drawn by them and this is income within the meaning of sections 2, 3 and 4 and therefore taxable in their hands.
In other words, their income is taxable whether or not they give it back to the colony. If a portion of it remains in their hands, it can be used by them in whatever way they like. However, they must pay the levy for doing business in this country. It has often been said that they are good people, that they ask nothing from this country and therefore we should not tax them. It is said that very few of them go to jail and that they mind their own business. All this is true, but it is also true that 99 per cent of all Canadians do not go to jail, and 99 per cent of those engaged in business wish the government would leave them alone.
However, the long tentacles of government reach into every facet of every Canadian's life. Sometimes I feel that these tentacles reach farther every day, so why exclude a particular group from their reach? It has been said that

they are good people. I will not argue whether they are good or bad. My argument rests on the fact that they live in Canada and many of them are Canadian citizens who do business in this country. Therefore, they should pay tax for doing business, whether or not they are good, whether or not they go to jail, etc.
It has been argued that members of the Amish or Men-nonite order in southern Ontario do not take advantage of what society has to offer them. What is interesting is that before they were to appear before the committee, some members of the committee did not want the Hutterites to appear so they quickly concluded the deliberations of the committee and the group did not appear. That was the committee members' mistake on that occasion. Perhaps it is true that the Amish group in southern Ontario do not depend on modern technological advances, but that cannot be said of the Hutterites in the three prairie provinces. They certainly take advantage of every new technological advance in carrying out their business. Certainly, they are not backward.
If I were a young, inexperienced farmer wanting to engage in the business of agriculture, one of the most knowledgeable men I could visit and from whom I could take advice regarding what is current, practical and applicable in agriculture in western Canada would be the Hutterite farming boss in the area. He knows what is going on and takes advantage of modern technological services provided to the farming community in Canada, as well as to the manufacturing industries with regard to flour and milling. They take advantage of our society and therefore I say they should pay the tax for belonging to our society.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to express my thoughts on Bill C-19, I should first of all like to make a few comments on clauses other than those that have been covered by the former speaker.
First of all, on the question of surviving spouse, I welcome the change in the bill that brings in the term "surviving spouse". I question, though, the adequacy of the 60 per cent which is being used as the base for the amount of the former pension that can be received by the surviving spouse. As mentioned by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, (Mr. Munro), while the expenses of the surviving spouse might not equal the total living expenses prior to the death of the spouse, surely 60 per cent is hardly adequate to meet the daily living needs of the person left behind. I would urge the minister very earnestly, that a re-examination of that 60 per cent be undertaken and that possible changes be examined very carefully in committee. Questions have also been raised as to whether the salaries of the husband and wife should not be combined when contributions are calculated so they could make a total contribution based on both salaries, regardless of whether that contribution is paid by the husband or the wife alone.
I should like to present that possibility to the minister for further examination.
April 18, 1974

I also welcome the change that removes the earnings test between ages 65 and 70 in order for a person to be eligible for Canada Pension Plan benefits. I believe in our society today, with a retirement age of 65, one should not be asked to prove whether one is entitled to a retirement pension. In view of the fact that the Canada Pension Plan is a contributory plan, largely by the employer and employee, and these contributions have been made for the benefit of the employee, that person should receive those benefits at age 65. That correlates with the age at which a person becomes eligible for the old age pension or the guaranteed income supplement. I believe it is only natural and right that these clauses should be introduced. I welcome them and commend the minister for introducing them.
As I am sure many hon. members realize, when I got to my feet this afternoon those matters were not going to be the main thrust of my argument. I find it strange to be in a position where I have to challenge the thoughts of a colleague who sits on the same side of the Speaker as myself, but that is what I intend to do today. First of all, the spokesman for my party on this bill very clearly defined that our party was going to endorse the legislation. He gave the commitment of our party that we favoured the changes and while we have certain questions on various points, by and large we are in agreement with the bill. I did not believe that the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) was a brave person, although I will give him credit for that as well, but I believed he was an honest person, stating very clearly the position that his party had taken. I endorse the position that the hon. member for Hillsborough has taken on behalf of our party.
When a bill is presented to the House, every member has a right in his own good conscience to either say he is in favour of the bill or is opposed to the bill. I do not remove that rignt or have any intention of removing it from those who disagree with me, but I do seriously question a person who uses arguments that, through innuendo, question the sincerity of others and uses that approach to block a bill. I seriously object to that kind of approach, Mr. Speaker.
The basis of the Canada Pension Plan has been the concept of universality, that a person who earns a taxable amount of income pays Canada Pension Plan premiums. This was also the basis of the argument which the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) used but I maintain, just as I did on Bill C-190, that the concept of universality was not used when the Canada Pension Plan was introduced. I do not know how you can say you have universality and yet you do not. It is an all or nothing type of thing. When the Canada Pension Plan was brought before this House and passed by this House, exceptions were given to people who made the vows of perpetual poverty and who were church employed. Since the date when the bill was passed, effective in 1966, there have been people in Canada who have had the option of exempting themselves on the basis of those two positions.
I am not quarrelling or questioning whether people exercise that option, but I say the option was there and is there today. I further say, Mr. Speaker, if you follow the argument, that this exception was given because of freedom of religion, then it makes no difference whatsoever
Canada Pension Plan
whether a person exercises that option. The option is in the bill, and it is in the law of Canada today.
If that is the basic concept of the argument I should like to read from the baptismal vows of the Hutterian Brethren, very specifically as to what their position is relative to these two clauses. The vows are that no one shall have any private possession any more: for one gives and surrenders himself to the Lord and His church with all that he has and is able to do, as it was in the original apostolic church, when no one said of his possessions that they were his own, but all things were held common to them.
The hon. member for Crowfoot mentioned the book "All Things Common" by Dr. Victor Peters. Dr. Peters takes the position, after extensive study of the Hutterians, specifically in Manitoba-and I know Dr. Peters-that the Hutterians are a group of people who are engaged in making a living for themselves. There is no question about that and I would maintain that almost all Canadians fall in that category. He maintains, too, that they hold all things common under the terms of Acts, chapter 2. This fact has also been based on a judgment in a case in Manitoba in which a number of former Hutterians left a colony. They took their case to court, arguing that the proportion they constituted of the male household heads of the colony of which they had formerly been members, entitled them to that same proportion of assets of that colony. Say for example, that they constituted 30 per cent of heads of households in the colony, then they should have received 30 per cent of the total assets of the colony when they left it. In the judgment the court very clearly stated, on the basis of the baptismal vows, that no one held anything but that the total membership held all goods and, as a result, those goods could not be divided because the common ownership had been given voluntarily by an adult at the age of accountability. One is not born a Hutterite. On reaching the age of accountability, a person can decide whether, by baptism, to become a Hutterite. That is an adult decision. It is not something which happens through birth.
How can you follow the argument of the hon. member, that you possess nothing as an individual? The Canada Pension Plan allows an individual to build up personal equity, just as if he were a member of a registered retirement savings plan. A person can build up equity by being a member of the plan, or by taking out a plan with an insurance company or similar type of company. At present we are talking of equity built up through membership in the Canada Pension Plan. How does an individual do this? He is given a social insurance number and makes contributions. The concept of individuality is in direct violation to the vows he has taken in the case in question, as an individual is held to own nothing.
Much of the previous speaker's argument was based on the fact that the Hutterites are not a church but, rather, a corporation or business. It is true that up until the 1960's they did not pay income tax. The government of Canada challenged that situation in the courts. The courts maintained the government's position. I firmly accept that decision. I am of the opinion that if Hutterites make a profit from farming, they should pay a tax. The difficulty with regard to the tax situation to which the hon. member

April 18, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
referred and the judgment to which he referred was this: up to that time, Hutterites had paid taxes as any other corporation pays them. The tax decision resulted in Hutterites being assessed and required to pay individually. This violated their concepts under which individuals do not gain wealth. They challenged the decision but lost the case. It is now a matter of history. I want to make it clear that they challenged that decision as a corporate body and not as individuals, because it has been held that an individual should not build up wealth for himself.
There is no evidence to show that Hutterites have not paid taxes, or that they have paid less or more than other Canadians. They are paying their taxes. That is not the real point at issue. If one argues that CPP premiums are a tax, one might argue that the Hutterites should pay such premiums. If you subscribe to the idea that you should render unto Caesar those things which are Caesar's and unto God those things which are God's, the tax should be rendered to Caesar-I do not know if that is an apt reference to the present government. That is the argument one might make.
I do not think that the basic concept of CPP premiums being a tax applies in this case. Why? The individual who pays CPP premiums will also get a personal benefit. The member who began this argument said that some people might even get windfall benefits. Further, the member made the innuendo that this bill treats some religions as being superior to others. He then destroyed that argument by saying that the Hutterites are not a church, not a religion, but a business. I do not know how they can be a religion and not a religion at the same time; but that is the point he tried to make. That is not the main point of my argument. I do not see how we can maintain that one religion is better than another. I do not see how you can bring that concept into this argument on what the bill does.
The government took the position, first enunciated by the former minister of national revenue and repeated by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), that Hutterites, effective January 1, 1972, would be exempt from the requirement to pay Canada Pension Plan premiums. Clauses relating to perpetual poverty and church employment were included in the original bill and therefore the present provision is not a special dispensation, as such clause has already been included. Therefore the government is fulfilling an obligation which was set out in the act it brought before the House in the 1960's.
Let me make one more argument. If my argument proves valid for January 1, 1972, it should prove valid for the time of the inception of the bill in 1966. What I am speaking of is this: We live in a democracy. Many have come here, to become part of the democratic framework of Canada. Canada took in many of these people who had been persecuted in other countries. Look at their history, and look at the persecutions under which they suffered in the 1500's, and at the places to which they were driven. At last they came to Canada; Canada gave them haven. All they asked of Canada was that they be allowed to follow their religion. Canada guaranteed them religious freedom. They did not ask for special favours. They did not say they would not become good citizens. They said they would obey the laws of this country, and they have. If you
[Mr. Epp.J
champion individual freedom, how can you champion it for one group but not for another? If certain freedoms are provided in a statute of Canada, how can you provide them for one group but not for another? All this bill does is finally rectify an inequity that has existed since the days the Canada Pension Plan bill was introduced.
As far as the democratic rights which this country gave to the Hutterites are concerned, I would like to point out that in Alberta, where there are a number of Hutterite colonies, there was a law that Hutterites could not build a Hutterite colony within 40 miles of an existing colony. It was called the 40 mile limit. The present government of Alberta rescinded that law. Under the Alberta bill of rights, the Alberta government took the stance that it was discriminatory legislation against a specific group.
Granted there are problems. I am not denying that. However, I think a number of us may have had neighbours with whom we might have had a problem or two. If we are honest about it, maybe some neighbours even had a problem with us. Alberta has rescinded the 40 mile law. There is a gentleman's agreement. I appreciate the difficulties in the implementation of it, but surely that is what life is all about. It is the responsibility of government to iron out differences between governments and individuals.
In Manitoba there has never been a law specifically relating to where Hutterites are to settle. We have a gentleman's agreement or the so-called 10 mile limit whereby Hutterites are asked not to build colonies within 10 miles of existing colonies. This has worked out quite well in Manitoba. Why? Because it has been based on co-operation between one group and another, between a government and its citizens. That trust is there. It worked with the former administration of Manitoba and it works with the present administration. Why? Because we want to make it work. If you are going to legislate and say that you are better than I or vice versa, you will run into trouble. You cannot do it. I maintain that this bill is trying to rectify that discrimination.
I would much rather discuss this bill on its merits but I have been forced into taking a position on clause 7 and that is why I spent most of my time debating that. I would like to conclude with this thought. If we want freedom, and if we want to do more than give lip service to the Bill of Rights, then we should be very careful and sincere about groups or individuals who feel certain actions would be a violation of conscience but not a violation of the laws of this country. Government should have the conscience and the ability to say a provision is discriminatory and remove the discrimination. That is the only way democracy will work.
I commend the minister for following up the promise made by the former Minister of National Revenue. I was disappointed in the previous session. Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in this debate and bring forward some ideas on an aspect of the bill which has not been touched on so far, that is, the general effect of the cost of the Canada Pension Plan in relation to its benefits in the future.
I am concerned to think we have been considering only the benefits which the CPP has in store for our citizens rather than its effect on our future economy. I might say that, speaking personally, I will probably receive benefits earlier than many people in this chamber. But in the course of this debate we have not touched on what the cost is likely to be, or upon the changes which are likely to be felt in the financial structure of the country. We have not questioned the effect of the proposed amendments or the actuarial soundness of the plan. We have tended to talk as though there were a bottomless pit of money rather than a fund designed to begin shrinking within the decade. I have heard it said by people who have studied it that the plan as now constituted will be bankrupt in four or five years. We have not considered the enormous amount of capital, under the control of the federal government and available for the use of the provinces; that, in fact, none of this money will be left to private enterprise for the development of Canada and to sustain economic growth. Enormous sums will be hived off from the general economy, taking no part in the national development.
I believe we have been guilty of assuming that dollars are the most important thing about a pension. In fact it is what those dollars can buy that matters. Merely giving dollars is of little value unless those dollars can purchase for their recipient the necessities of life. One comment about the inflation in Germany after the Second World Waristicks;in|my mindjThe housewives there said: We took our money to the store in baskets and brought the food home in our pockets. More and more, workers and employers regard the CPP contributions as a tax. With the emptying of the fund it looks less like a contributory, self-supporting pension scheme and more like a transfer payment. I have no quarrel with this essentially, as long as we know what we are doing and where we are going. We need to examine the consequences of this legislation, particularly to the young, including those who have not yet made their first CPP contribution, and demonstrate an awareness of the cost burden in the years ahead. To pass this legislation blindly without discussing these aspects of the plan would be a hasty action indeed.
This afternoon we have been discussing the aspect of the bill which concerns a religious group. These considerations are important. But if we do not deal with the financial aspects, the situation in the years ahead will be perilous. The magnitude of the benefits that the Canada Pension Plan will bring is quite staggering compared with what those affected-that is, the middle and lower income groups-might customarily expect. The minister outlined the very generous benefits that will be accorded those who contribute to the plan. If a contributor in 1966, at the onset of the plan, was earning $4,000, then was earning $5,000 a year in 1974 and $7,000 in 1985, and be then retired, had the

plan remained as it was originally he would have received only $162 a month whereas he will now receive $223 a month because a cost of living index relationship has been built into the plan.
Then, the minister pointed out, and I think quite rightly, in calculating the entire income of a single wage earner or a couple, that a little over a year ago the maximum income derived from the Canada Pension Plan and old age security would have been about $240 a month, whereas today it is $320 a month. By 1980 this same couple will receive $525 a month, and by 1985 well over $700 a month. This assumes that the wage earner makes $7,000 a year during his last working year. In addition to that, the cost of living index will be incorporated into the plan, and with the increase now running at 10 per cent hon. members can see a truly large amount of money is involved. The cost of giving our retired people pensions will be a large element in our over-all social structure.
The minister quoted an example which showed that in 10 years a couple would increase their pension from $300 a month, with one of the couple working, to $700 a month. If he were to save this amount of money, the difference in amount would be quite staggering. Many years ago, in attempting to understand insurance annuities and so on, I was informed that it took approximately $1,000 of annuity at age 70 to give an individual $10 a month, for his life expectancy. At 65 an individual required an annuity of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $1,300 to provide him with $10 a month.
Let us see what the Canada Pension Plan and old age security will do for the couple earning a maximum of $7,000 a year, with only one person earning. This single wage earner would have had to save somewhere in the neighbourhood of $40,000 to $50,000 in order to get a comparable annuity for himself. This is to say nothing of the very great benefits the CPP confers upon widows, dependent children and the disabled. I am not saying that this is not right, but I point out that the Canada Pension Plan as constituted, along with old age security, represents a transfer payment of a considerable amount.
In addition, no private plan would carry with it the cost of living index, as the CPP does. In fact, the $700 a month forecast by the minister with the cost of living index incorporated into the CPP and old age security that a couple would receive in 1985 may well rise as high as $1,200 a month. Perhaps this couple will need that amount then, but nevertheless this is an indication of the actuarial scope of the Canada Pension Plan.

speechtext:
That an order of the House do issue for a copy of the latest evaluation report of the Canada Manpower Mobility Program.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am not surprised the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) and the government have refused to agree to the publishing of a copy of the latest evaluation report of the Canada Manpower Mobility Program as this is in line with the general policy of this government over the years to give members of parliament and of the public as little information as possible. The Department of Manpower and Immigration spends almost $600 million for its work in the field of manpower and immigration, and I exclude from that figure the amount which is spent by the Unemployment Insurance Commission which reports to parliament and the people of Canada through the minister. I will confine myself and my remarks to those programs conducted by the department in the field of manpower and immigration.
When one looks at this year's estimates, he sees that the department has estimated its expenditures for the year
1554

April 18, 1974
Manpower Mobility Program
1974-75 in the amount of $599 million. If one looks at the breakdown, he will see that it will be spending some $315 million on manpower program activities, and when one looks at the utilization and operation of those programs he sees that the estimated expenditure amounts to almost $300 million. Let us assume for the sake of argument that this department is doing a superlative job. I suggest that the officials are still human beings and can make mistakes, and if a member of parliament is in touch with his constituents he will know from speaking with people who have been in touch with manpower training schools and community colleges that from time to time departmental officials make decisions they feel are arbitrary or that they cannot understand.
Some weeks ago I raised a question with the minister in respect of the amount of money the department contracts to turn over to the provinces for manpower training. This amount seems to have been cut this year in respect of training projects by something in the neighbourhood of 10 per cent in almost every province. That may be a good decision as perhaps we have been spending too much money in the training of too many people, but there has been no evidence made public or to members of parliament at meetings of the standing committee, or to provincial governments, that would substantiate such a decision. This is a unilateral ukase on the part of the Department of Manpower and Immigration. Without suggesting that officials of the department were wrong, they should be ready to explain and justify what is being done. They should be ready to show the people of Canada and members of this and provincial governments what has led them to the decision to cut the expenditures in respect of these programs, or the adoption of new ones.
What has bothered me for a number of years is the seeming desire on the part of the government to keep everything quiet, hidden and secret. It may be that the expenditure of something in the neighbourhood of $500 million is necessary, worthwhile and justified, but if that is so the department should be willing and eager to give this information to the public. The department should not have to be urged or coerced.
Let me give a specific case. We have a mobility program operated by the department of manpower under the jurisdiction of the minister through which a person with a particular skill can be encouraged to move to another area where there is a requirement for that skill if that individual cannot find suitable work in his own city, town or village. This might involve a miner from Cape Breton being moved to Sudbury or an electrician being moved from an area where there is no work for one with such a skill to Vancouver or another city where there is work. This is a voluntary program and no worker is forced to move because there is no work for him in his field in his own city or province.
The whole purpose of the mobility program is to encourage workers who have skills which cannot be put to use in the area where they reside to move to places where there is a need for skilled workers in that field, and where the likelihood is that such workers can obtain meaningful employment at satisfactory rates of pay. I support that program, but I think the people of Canada are entitled to as much assurance as possible that it is operating success-

fully and is actually achieving the purpose of finding employment for people in other areas when they are not able to find employment in their own cities or provinces.
I would hate to think of a person who had been encouraged to move from say Cape Breton Island or Halifax to Sudbury or Toronto, because supposedly there was a job waiting for him there, finding, after having worked for a month, two months, three months or six months that there was no longer any work for him and that he was unemployed in a strange city and a strange province. I am not saying this is what happens, but it is a possibility. I would hate to think that a worker who was encouraged to move by way of being given a mobility grant might find that the employer did not live up to the conditions. Perhaps the pay scale did not turn out to be what had been promised, or the working conditions were not as stated or decent housing was not provided after he had been promised that it would be available. This is the type of problem which I submit can and does occur. I do not say this in criticism of the government. The only way in which there could be no mistakes in respect of a mobility program would be if there were no such program.
I am not opposed to a mobility program. On the contrary I think it should be expanded. How can we know that the program is working in the way in which it was designed to work? How can we know whether the officials administering the program are doing a job or are doing it properly? I submit we cannot know if the government is determined as it seems to be to hide everything. I suggest, as I suggested on other occasions and I hope I will be more successful this time, that there is no reason the government should keep secret these house surveys, these detailed reports merely because the position is taken that they are confidential and therefore cannot be disclosed. On the contrary, I say we require much more information, much more openness and much more desire on the part of the government to tell the people of Canada what the government is doing and why it is doing it. The cost of government increases from year to year. The number of people employed by governments, federal, provincial and municipal, increases from year to year. It does not seem to matter whether the government involved is Liberal as it is federally, Conservative as it is in Newfoundland and in Ontario or NDP as it is in Manitoba, Saskatchewan or British Columbia. In any event, the cost of government increases.
The number of public servants employed by governments increases. I say this is inevitable so long as the people want government to provide more services. I do not object to it, but I believe governments must be more accountable for the responsibilities they undertake. I think governments must have not only a duty but a responsibility to account to the people for what they are doing and to inform the people what they are doing and why they are doing it. The people should be informed concerning how programs are operating, the success of the programs and so on. It is for this reason, after becoming aware of the fact that the government has received an evaluation report on the Canada Manpower Mobility Program, that I moved this motion. I would urge the government to stop hiding things. When it hides such reports the
April 18, 1974

government convinces members of parliament and members of the public that they should wonder what is going on. I believe some members on the government side might agree with me in this regard but they cannot say so because they are members of the government. I do not say this in a critical way because I assume if I were a member of a government party I would feel the same way.
Stories are told about people ripping off the unemployment insurance fund, drawing welfare benefits to which they are not entitled and so on. One may hear stories about farmers receiving assistance under some farm legislation to which they are not entitled. If hon. members doubt what I am saying they need simply tune in on any hotline radio program in order to find out the type of feeling people have about governments, federal, provincial and municipal. In this way hon. members would realize that people are concerned about the way in which governments operate. I suggest to members on the government side that it is not surprising that people feel the way they do. On the contrary, it is surprising that more of them do not feel the same way.
If one wishes to see the extent to which people can become upset, or the extent to which they can come to believe that governments and elected members of a legislature or state or federal government can fail to do the job, one might simply look at the various polls being conducted in the United States concerning how the people of the United States feel about their President and their elected representatives in the House of Representatives or in the United States Senate. In a recent poll it was indicated that less than 25 per cent of the people believed their elected representatives are doing a good job. A large part of the disillusionment in this regard is that, rightly or wrongly, the people believe that President Nixon has failed to give them the facts concerning the Watergate affair. I am not suggesting for a moment that the people of Canada have as poor an opinion of their elected representatives as the American people have of theirs. I do not believe this is the case. I hope it is not. One should not be surprised, however, if Canadian citizens express concern or surprise about the way they are being governed if they are so consistently and deliberately kept in the dark concerning what is going on.
I wish to conclude my few remarks by simply appealing to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) to stop being so determined about hiding the real facts concerning what is going on in his department. If he believes, as I think the minister should, that his department, his officials and the people who work in his department are trying their best to do a good job and on the whole are succeeding, then the minister should have no hesitation in agreeing to table this kind of report so that in this area the people of Canada would be able to see whether the program is working and the way in which it is working.

General Principle
To enable Members of Parliament to secure factual information about the operations of government to carry our their parliamentary duties and to make public as much factual information as possible consistent with effective administration, the protection of the security of the state, rights to privacy and other such matters, government papers, documents and consultant reports should be produced on Notice of Motion for the Production of Papers unless falling within the categories outlined below in which case an exemption is to be claimed from production.
What we normally hear is a categorical denial of the exemptions without treating them on an individual basis. This, in fact, was the complaint registered by the President of the Privy Council when he stated this principle and exceptions to it. I will take one of them as an example, namely, "legal opinions or advice provided for the use of the government." I do not think anybody in his right mind, unless he is being totally political, can disagree with that exception. Another one is "papers, the release of which would be detrimental to the security of the state". There are 16 such exceptions. When we hear complaints by opposition members that a particular document should be made available or made public, it seems to me that we should answer on the basis of any of the 16 exemptions, and if they should be attacked, that is where the opposition parties should move in.

This is one of the main areas of interest in notices of motions which ask departments to produce internal memoranda. I will not read the whole article by Professor Knight but I think that a portion of it would indicate the thrust of the thinking of the Professor who is a recognized expert in the field. He said it in 1966 but I suggest it is equally true today:
The civil servant may feel, too, that he must avoid placing on record anything which is likely to offend or cut across the interests of any individual or group in the community. This could affect not only the generalist administrator having a policy advisory role, but also the large body of officials whose work is concerned essentially with matters of a technical or professional nature. An officer who prepared a report on, say, the relative merits of butter and margarine, might well find himself the centre of a political controversy long before any decision about subsidies or production restrictions had been reached at the political level. Even if he wished to defend himself and had the ability as a controversialist to do so, the means open to him to do so would hardly be adequate.
So we place our civil servants and people who were retained to advise government departments in an untenable position. If they are told that a particular study or

report they are preparing for the consideration of the government on a policy that it has adopted or proposes to adopt or a program that has been in effect for a couple of years will not be kept confidential, I suggest that this weakens the report. If they give a report that they anticipate will be kept confidential and it is then not kept confidential, then I think you do a disservice to the individual who has been retained to give you that report.
There may be a series of suggestions in this report on the mobility program that the government would reject out of hand as not being consistent with the thrust of intention of the particular program. On that basis you would have an individual who has made a report contrary to a government position. A cabinet minister has the ultimate responsibility for making the decision, and then you would have a crossfire between the deputy minister, or whoever prepared the report, and the minister becoming a matter of public record.
I suggest that this would weaken the parliamentary system. This is going to the very root of what the parliamentary system is all about, that the man or individual who has the prime responsibility for a piece of legislation or a program is the minister himself, and it is up to him to cull out what he thinks is good in the program and then face the House of Commons on that subject. He then, of course, has to answer during examination of the estimates for the money that is put out on a particular program; he has to indicate its strength and defend its weakness. That responsibility in the parliamentary system falls upon the elected member who in this instance is a cabinet minister.
Mr. Speaker, I understand that there are many other members who wish to speak on the subject. I was going to elaborate, for the edification of the hon. member who moved the motion, on the general principles and exemptions that were indicated by the President of the Privy Council on March 15. I thought, therefore, he might have drawn to the attention of his colleague why this particular report falls within the exemptions that were enumerated in the debate.
Recognizing that our time is limited, Mr. Speaker, I will yield the floor to others who wish to participate.
