The general principle must not be overlooked. As the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton. expressed it, information should always be provided to members of parliament if it will assist them in discharging their duties and not endanger the security of the state or of individuals within the state. Obviously, information about the Canada Manpower Mobility Program would assist members of parliament in discharging their foremost responsibility. Such information would not endanger the security of the state or of individuals within the state.
Government expenditures have reached a level which is nothing short of atrocious. The government is intruding more and more into the private sector and into the lives of individuals. The government is budgeting for expenditures of some $22 billion per year, or $1,000 for every man, woman and child in this country. I am not saying that $1,000 is spent on every man, woman and child; merely that the government's budget is huge when $1,000 per man, woman and child has to be budgeted for. If the parliamentary system is to be weakened, it will be weakened, not by disclosing information to which members of parliament are entitled but by withholding it. When you hide things from members of parliament, representatives duly elected of the people, you are saying, "We have something to hide."
If you have a good reason to withhold information, because disclosure would imperil the security of the state, individuals within the state or their right to privacy, that is one thing. On the other hand, when you withhold information you are encouraging people to fear what the government is doing, to be suspicious about how their money is spent. You weaken their confidence in democracy, confidence which is necessary if a democratic society is to function, if the government is to be respected and if it is to discharge its responsibilities to the people. This it can do only in an atmosphere of co-operation and when it feels it has the support of the people.
I join the hon. member in suggesting that whenever possible documents relating to government activity which will assist members of parliament discharge their responsibilities should be made available to members on the conditions previously referred to. Mr. Speaker, the motion in the name of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) reads:
That an order of the House do issue for a copy of the latest evaluation report of the Canada Manpower Mobility Program.
When the hon. member originally requested the latest evaluation report on April 10, I replied to his request in

these words as recorded at page 1331 of Hansard for that date:
-the evaluation report of the Canada Manpower Mobility Program was prepared jointly by the department and the Treasury Board secretariat as an internal working document for their exclusive use. I would therefore ask the member to withdraw his motion.
The hon. member was not willing to withdraw; hence, we are debating the matter today. This motion raises one of the greatest issues which confronts a democratic people-the right of people to know what is going on in their country. Although it may not be evident from hon. members' speeches, this is an exceedingly complex question: it is not a simple question to which a simple reply can be given. To show my general outlook on the subject, may I quote from the third report of the Special Committee on Statutory Instruments placed before the House in 1969. I had the privilege of being chairman of that committee. In the introduction to this report, the committee said:
This report is based on the assumption that public knowledge of governmental activities is the basis of all control of delegated legislation. For parliamentary democracy is a system of government which requires that the executive be responsible to the legislature and that both be accountable to the people, and there can be neither responsibility nor accountability where there is no knowledge of what has been done. In political matters knowledge is the beginning of power, and its lack, impotence.
I stand by those words which I had the privilege of creating earlier.

speechtext:
If the hon. member for Rocky Mountain had cared to attend the committee hearings, he might
Manpower Mobility Program
have had an opportunity of finding the facts. The minister was most open in presenting the facts. Members do not need to have the actual report presented as an internal document. They are able to question the minister about the same area as that covered by the document. They can ask his views and those of the departmental officials as to how well the department is functioning. In that form they get exactly the same information.
We are here discussing more a point of procedure than a point of substance. We on this side are not saying parliament should not have this information. We are saying we will not present an internal departmental document because that kind of documentation, in a case such as this, would establish a precedent which could lead to the breaking down of effective democratic government. Members opposite have other ways of finding out the same information. The best way is to criticize and question the minister when he comes before the committee on his estimates. They have not done that with regard to this program, yet they come here and ask us to hand them on a platter information which they have not taken the trouble to ascertain. I do not think that is good parliamentary practice. I will be charitable and suggest that perhaps this is the fault of the researchers they have hired. I think this is the best way to leave that point.
What is it the Canada Manpower Mobility Program does? What kind of concern would the department have in authorizing an analysis of this kind? The basic principle of the Canada Manpower Mobility Program is to provide financial assistance for unemployed, underemployed or persons about to become unemployed to enable them to relocate in areas closest to their homes where there are suitable job opportunities. It may be used to help the worker who is without a job because his skill is not required in his own area, or the worker who is underemployed in a job where his skills are unused or outdated. It can also help the person who needs to improve his earning capacity by attending federally-sponsored training courses not offered near his home, or persons who need specialized Manpower service not available in their home area.
The program complements other measures to promote high productivity. Assistance under the program forms an integral part of other federal government departments' adjustment activities, namely, those of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, the Newfoundland fisheries resettlement program and other provincial schemes. The aim of the Canada Manpower Mobility Program is not to subsidize all workers' mobility but, rather, to assist and serve as an incentive to those who need to move but require financial assistance.
The Manpower mobility regulations provide four types of assistance. First, exploratory grants to enable workers to search for employment in another area. Second, relocation grants to facilitate permanent relocation of workers and their families. Third, trainee travel and commuting allowances to enable adults to take occupational training in a locality other than that in which they reside. Fourth, special travel grants to obtain special Manpower services required to facilitate entry into productive employment.

I am pleased to advise that these changes have made the relocation of workers and their families more successful than previously.
Our evaluation of the exploratory grants program indicates that approximately one in every two workers is successful in obtaining a job during the first exploratory trip.
The information is there being made available to parliament and to the public. The opposition just has not been able to recognize the forest for the trees which it has put in the way. Obviously, the kind of thing with which a study of this kind would be concerned would in large part be the question of disincentive. Is there any disincentive imposed by such a program? In the absence of the program would the worker have remained unemployed in his locality? Would he have placed an increased demand on unemployment insurance and social welfare? Obviously, this is the type of thing such a study would have attempted to answer. These are the very types of questions to which the minister was attempting to provide answers during his appearance before the standing committee on estimates. He also stated at that time:
The second change introduced was to increase the home owner's allowance from $500 to $1,500 to enhance the success of relocation for families who did not own a home. Since the revised home owner's allowances went into effect, there has been an increase of approximately 18 per cent in the number of workers who were able to purchase a home in their relocation area ensuring the success and permanency of the relocation.
The vote which was approved by the committee was for $9.2 million. That was a week or so ago. To continue with the analysis of the problem and the type of service given by the Manpower Mobility Program, a program about which the opposition might have asked questions if they had wished, I shall give a fuller explanation of the exploratory grants program to which I referred in mentioning the changes which the minister announced. The exploratory grants program covers the cost of return transportation of the worker to the nearest area considered by Canada Manpower to hold reasonable prospects for employment. Interviews for the client with prospective employers are often arranged by the department. The grant also includes a living allowance of $13 a day, for a maximum of five days, while the worker is in the area actively seeking work.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock I was dealing with certain aspects of the Canada Pension Plan. Now, after the supper hour, I am happy to see that so many members, including the minister, were able to tear themselves away from the hockey game. If the minister could get the bill passed I am sure we would unanimously agree to deal with hockey in the next couple of hours instead of the football bill we may be faced with.
In setting aside people's savings under the Canada Pension Plan we are bringing about a vast change in the savings patterns of individuals. I suggest that savings by the group over 50 years of age is now much less important than in the past. With the present very high rate of inflation this large group is not able to protect itself by ordinary plans. The minister himself pointed this out in Toronto when making a statement according to a report in the Globe and Mail, before the Canada Pension Plan conference held in November of last year. He said, "When the value of the current $105 in old age security is added, we can discuss adequacy with a clear conscience".
I think he then drew attention to the important question behind this legislation: what is adequacy? If the old age pension and Canada pension together are adequate for an individual, then it seems to be of little value for him to save as well for his retirement. Has the Canada Pension Plan made private pension plans redundant or largely made private pension plans redundant? The minister went on to point out at this conference that it is a matter of public concern that only 40 per cent of Canadians are covered-this is quite true-and that in many ways the Canada Pension Plan can cover the whole field better than private plans. On the other hand, will the Canada Pension Plan be a truly funded plan, or will it be increasingly funded from general revenue with little relationship between what one puts in and what one takes out?
It also seems important that those who are retiring within the next 10 or 15 years take a look at their own savings from the point of view of spending them for their own personal benefit, rather than using them as an income supplement, since the Canada Pension Plan presumably will be quite adequate.
One other factor in comparing the Canada Pension Plan with private pension plans is that the Canada Pension Plan lends money to the provinces, and they alone are the recipients of CPP funds. If provinces are able to borrow from the CPP without having to go to the market for funds, then in my opinion this makes for an absence of the normal restraint that is placed on provincial spending. For instance, if a provincial government has a program that
April 18, 1974

has to be funded, say a hydro development project, then if they go to the market to raise the money I think the project will be designed better and more thought will be put into it, whereas if the province is able to borrow from the Canada Pension Plan fund almost at will, there is an "easy come, easy go" attitude.
The Canada Pension fund also provides a huge reservoir of cash which is independent of the business cycle; hence over-all government spending, taxing measures and fiscal policy are beyond the normal restraint exercised by the legislature. Often people criticize free enterprise for its failings, but if there is a great deal of intergovernment borrowing that short-circuits the free market, then the free market is being jeopardized. If a province needs money, it should deal directly with the market. Borrowing from the Canada Pension Plan conflicts with two different interests-the needs of the provincial treasury and the rights of contributors to the pension fund.
Naturally, a provincial government prefers to borrow at the most advantageous rate, so any borrowing from the fund would, from the point of view of the fund, be disadvantageous. If there were an incentive on the part of the managers of the fund to obtain maximum yield from investments, then the productive and rewarding sectors of the economy would benefit. It is my understanding that the managers of the Quebec Pension Plan fund have had a much better return on their investments than have the managers of the Canada Pension Plan fund, and this is to be commended. I think the managers of the CPP fund should look at what has been done with the investments made by the QPP fund.
The accumulation of savings capital in the Canada Pension Plan fund, in private pension funds, in mutual funds and insurance funds is to the disadvantage of certain segments of the country. The pooling of investment capital tends to be in the large financial centres of the country, where it is managed by a few people, the large financial conglomerates, to the detriment of rural areas. It has been suggested that Canada Pension Plan funds might contribute to the financing of business and other enterprises in the free market instead of this being the prerogative of the provinces, and I think more study should be done along these lines.
I think the important thing to discuss when we consider the Canada Pension Plan is what effect it is going to have on savings and how best pension funds can be invested in this country to bring in as much income as possible for contributors. Above all, this large pool of money should be used in the most constructive way in the financial and industrial sectors of the economy.
With those few words, Mr. Speaker, I will close. In committee I hope we will find some answers to the many actuarial problems that this bill presents.

speechtext:
In its own small way, this football controversy seems to epitomize the central dilemmas of our 100 years as a nation. The type of debate we have been witnessing seems to me symbolic of our history, too. It is the kind of debate we have had many times in the past. So many of the same old arguments keep popping up, arguments that we really should have settled and put to rest a long time ago.
We hear about the principles of free enterprise and free competition in the marketplace. We are told that the state

Canadian Professional Football should not interfere with private business unless, of course, private business requests state help. We are bombarded with lectures about people's freedom of choice and freedom of movement and other fundamental rights. I am not denying the values of free enterprise and competition, and I am not making fun of the people who advance these arguments; but they are not absolutes and never have been, at least not in Canadian history. As Canadians, we have always had to acknowledge the consequences of living alongside a much richer and more powerful neighbour. We have always had to be aware of what could happen and, in some instances, what has happened by allowing our neighbour unrestrained access to what is ours. While we have received literally countless benefits from our close relationship with the United States, we must also recognize that we have paid a price: too often, in the past, the demise or disappearance of Canadian institutions in the face of much greater economic and demographic powers.
This, then, is one of our traditional dilemmas as Canadians: how to remain open to, but not dominated by, the influence of our great neighbour. Ever since confederation we have tried to resolve that dilemma by taking conscious decisions at the federal level, either to impose restraints on foreign influences or to create or maintain institutions of our own. Without such conscious decisions we would have no national railway system today; our railways would probably run north and south along what we are told are natural geographic lines. Without such a conscious decision by the parliament of Canada we would today have no national broadcasting system and our radio and television stations would likely be local affiliates of NBC or CBS.
In both instances, in respect of the railways and the CBC, a decision to simply tie in with the American continental system would have been cheaper and possibly even more politically popular at the time. But the decisions to create and maintain our own Canadian systems, even with the extra costs involved, were seen, correctly, as part of the price of national sovereignty at that time. I am not talking only about decisions made "away back when;" the Foreign Policy Review Act, passed by this parliament, is one more recent example of federal intervention to control or regulate foreign domination in some sectors of our economy.
So there is nothing unprecedented or arbitrary in the government's present action to protect Canadian football, as some have charged. The legislation now before the House is in fact no different in principle from legislation that already protects many other Canadian enterprises. We are not trying to exclude foreign influences in football, but simply to control them. And I think even the most staunch advocate of free enterprise would agree there are times when the government must be prepared to protect the legitimate interests of all Canadians.
In this regard, Canada has traditionally been much more liberal than most countries in the world in maintaining an open door, especially for professionals. American musicians and other performing artists still have a much easier time coming to Canada to work than, say, Canadian musicians have in going to the United States. The same is true in many other fields; consulting, for example.

One group of Canadian professionals, hockey players, have for 50 years experienced little trouble in entering the United States, but that situation could very well change in the next few years as the Americans begin developing enough professional calibre players of their own. In fact, many Canadians were effectively barred from playing U.S. college hockey by a recent decision of the NCAA, the governing body of American collegiate sports. The NCAA made a ruling in August, 1971, concerning professionalism which really applied only to Canadian Junior "A" players, and the stated purpose of the ruling was to encourage more American players. So this is not a one-way street; it clearly works both ways.
The flow of skilled people across international borders is rarely a case of simple supply and demand as some would have us believe. It involves many other questions, among them, as in U.S. college hockey, a policy of developing home-grown talent and the effects of unlimited foreign players on that development. But even if we agree that there are legitimate areas for government or state intervention simply to keep us Canadian, we then find ourselves confronted by another dilemma. What kind of Canada do we want? One in which the rich just get richer and the poor stay poor, or one in which there is a conscious effort toward equalization and interdependence? Again, this dilemma seems to be epitomized in the last few weeks' debate about football.
I have received telegrams of support for the government's position from the mayors of many of our major cities, Calgary, Ottawa, Hamilton, Regina, Winnipeg and Edmonton, which are six cities in the Canadian Football League. I have not received similar telegrams from the mayors of our three largest cities, Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver. Is this just a coincidence? I do not think so. I am not pointing a finger at the mayors of our big cities or accusing them of anything. Like us in parliament, they are elected to look after the interests of their constituents as they see them. Again, this split seems to reflect the traditional stresses and perhaps the lack of common interests between our large urban areas and our smaller centres- the kind of alienation reporters like to write about.
Those of us who live in big Canadian cities tend to forget the real nature of the problem. We know that if we did not have the CFL we would have some other kind of professional football. We have the population, the money and the markets, and we like to think of ourselves as big league in every way. But, as Canadians, do we have the right to say that what happens elsewhere does not matter to us? As members of parliament, do we not have an obligation to care about what the CFL means to all those other Canadians? What does it mean? I was on a CBC radio phone-in show a few weeks ago and a young man in Halifax said something that impressed me as a statement of what it means. There are as yet, as hon. members know, no CFL teams in the maritimes. This young man told me he often remains up at night to watch the games on television, even games from Vancouver which do not start until midnight, his time. He said the reason is that watching Canadian football makes him "feel connected with the rest of the country".

What about Alberta and Saskatchewan? Somebody earlier mentioned Alberta. Over the last two months, as this House is aware, those two provinces felt they were entitled to the international price of $10.50 a barrel for their oil. The government's position was that it was all right for them to sell their own oil at that price abroad, but that selling it at that price domestically would have serious repercussions in respect of fuel costs to Canadians as a whole. As the House knows, they settled for $6.50 a barrel, a long way from the international price, in the interests of all Canadians-but especially, let us face it, the interests of consumers in the large eastern markets where the population is. This, of course, was not an isolated instance of Canadian provinces or regions agreeing to a reasonable compromise for the common good. As this House knows, it is precisely that kind of give-and-take that has made this country a viable entity. I am, therefore, disappointed when a member of Montreal's civic government is reported as saying, on the WFL question: What do we owe the west? Look how they held us up on the oil.
I am also disappointed when a Montreal sportswriter says:
If Marc Lalonde has his way, the people of Toronto and Montreal will be compelled by law forever to accept an inferior brand of football simply because people living in smaller cities can't afford big league entertainment.
The basic assumption here seems to be that if it is Canadian, it is inferior-an assumption I for one am not prepared to accept.
Some hort. Members: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext:
Nor do I think any of us should accept that football teams are necessarily superior just because they play in a league which calls itself the World Football League and has yet to play a single game. Nor can any of us believe that football teams are somehow better or more big league only because they are located in cities bigger than some CFL cities. If that were the case, then Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal would dominate the CFL competitively-something we know they don't do. There is also some irony in the fact that the most vocal opposition to the government's policy of protecting Canadian football has been centred in that part of the country that throughout our history has benefited most from the protection of its own industries. That includes the sports equipment industry.
The protection of Canadian football is not a local issue. It is not a regional issue. It is not a partisan issue. In our view, it is an issue that effects all parts of Canada and all Canadians and it will be decided, not in the press or on radio or television but by the parliament of Canada.
The bill now before the House is designed to protect Canadian football. To that end it embodies the position adopted by the government of Canada in November, 1972, and the policy first stated publicly by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), a policy that has remained unchanged since that time. The Canadian football bill is a short and straight-forward piece of legislation which embodies only those provisions necessary to achieve its purpose. The bill, as proposed, would limit professional football in Canada solely to teams from Canadian leagues. It provides that a minimum of 55 per cent of the players in
Canadian Professional Football Canadian professional football will be Canadians, and that no team will have on its roster more than 15 players who are not qualified Canadians, whichever results in the lesser number of players who are not qualified Canadians. That formula will apply for the 1974 playing season and until December 31 of this year.
After December 31, 1974, the minimum number of qualified Canadian players will rise to at least 60 per cent or 15 players who are not qualified Canadians, again whichever results in the lesser number of players who are not qualified Canadians. The bill contains no retroactive measures. It will not create a monopoly situation since it will allow for the establishment of other Canadian professional football leagues so long as all professional teams meet the criteria of the legislation. The bill will allow the CFL to expand to other Canadian cities and it will even allow the establishment of second CFL teams in major cities such as Toronto.
We believe these measures will not only protect Canadian football but will also allow it to grow and develop while maintaining its Canadian character. Like the Canadian content regulations in broadcasting and other portions of our cultural life, this legislation is aimed at strengthening the Canadian content of our football by giving more players a chance to play professionally in their own country.
As one who believes that Canadian football must grow if it is to survive and prosper, I have welcomed the CFL's decision to expand into any area which could support a franchise. The CFL's eastern conference is at this time seriously considering the application of a group in London, Ontario, and the Hamilton club has agreed to waive its rights in that territory, subject to acceptance of the London application. The CFL has also indicated its willingness to consider expansion into Halifax-Dartmouth and would like to review applications from interested parties in that area proposing teams either privately or community-owned.
As I announced last week after introducing the Canadian football bill, steps are being taken to allow more Toronto people to see their team's home games. This has not been possible for many because of sell-out crowds and local television blackouts. Plans are going ahead to expand the Toronto stadium, but that may take some time and still might not meet the demand for seats. Accordingly, the new owner of the Argonauts has undertaken to lift the local television blackout on an experimental basis, beginning this season, when it is established in advance that games are sold out. No individual CFL club can make such a decision on its own without the approval of the other clubs in the league, but the CFL commissioner has undertaken to put the proposition before the other CFL clubs and encourage them to accept it.
The CFL has also given assurances that it will look favourably on the possibility of all-star games between the CFL and other leagues, whether played in Canada or abroad. We should also note that the bill does not in any way restrict Canadian professional teams from playing exhibition games against teams from other leagues, either in Canada or outside the country.
It is the government's position to uphold and to strengthen the Canadian character of our football. We believe that the growing number of positions for Canadian

players assured by the present bill will greatly stimulate the development of high-calibre players across the country. To encourage the broadly based program that such development will require, my department has recently agreed with the philosophy of the Canadian Amateur Football Association stated in its proposed seven-year master plan for the development of Canadian football. The plan aims at greater participation and greater involvement in all areas-coaching, training, officiating and playing.
Through my department the government will be supporting the appointment of a technical director for amateur football. Through this measure, football becomes the first non-Olympic sport to receive such support. Through its seven-year master plan the CAFA hopes to increase the number of Canadians participating in football from the present estimated 250,000 to about 600,000, in this way both broadening the participation base and improving the quality of players through various technical programs.
Such efforts would be ineffective if we did not at the same time maximize opportunities for such players to play professional football in Canada. My department, through the fitness and amateur sport directorate, now funds the CAFA by means of normal annual grants for its ongoing programs, such as executive meetings, annual general meetings, Canadian eastern and western junior football playoffs and the Canadian junior finals-what we call the Junior Grey Cup.
My department has also agreed to fund a national officials' training clinic in which officials from all parts of Canada will participate. In the 1973-74 academic year, grants in aid to the student athletes program are providing scholarships for 27 outstanding football players to allow them to continue their academic studies at a number of Canadian universities. Those 27 football scholarships are the largest number awarded in any single sport. They represent a value of close to $50,000, which is in addition to the other football programs funded by the federal government.
I should also note that the Canadian Football League, even though it has no jurisdiction over amateur football in Canada, provides a direct national grant of $50,000 a year to the CAFA as well as another approximately $110,000 in cash and in kind through coaching clinics, try-out camps and other services by the CFL clubs to the amateur programs in their areas. I sincerely doubt that any American league would do the same for Canadians.
It is obvious from what I have said that the federal government's interest in Canadian football is not confined only to the CFL, its nine teams and 300 or so professional players. The CFL is merely the most highly visible part of the Canadian football pyramid which is made up of approximately 250,000 players. So when we talk about protecting football we are not discussing only the CFL, although any weakening of the CFL would have implications for the CAFA's amateur programs as well.
Saskatchewan's Premier Blakeney pointed out last month in a news release that if teams in United States leagues started to cut into general Canadian football revenues, the professional teams would not be the only ones to suffer. He noted:

Teams such as the Saskatchewan Roughriders spend thousands of dollars a year encouraging high school and junior football in Saskatchewan. They give young Canadian football players a chance to play top quality football in their own country for the benefit of Canadians.
In short, whatever threatens the CFL threatens Canadian football in general. I will not dwell on the reasons why we believe the CFL is worth protecting and preserving. I will simply list them. The CFL is the only completely Canadian-controlled professional sports league in Canada. It consists solely of Canadian teams. Even under its present regulations, more than half its players are Canadians. The present number of more than 150 Canadian players will, of course, increase under the bill before the House. Its teams stretch across the country from Vancouver to Montreal. Thousands of other Canadians benefit indirectly from its activities. It provides a consistently high level of competition; seven different teams have played in the last four Grey Cup games.
In CFL cities, football is not merely another branch plant operation of the North American entertainment industry. It provides a focus for deep community involvement and civic and provincial pride. Finally, there is the Grey Cup-a Canadian tradition that dates back to 1909, and since 1921 has led to a great east-west rivalry. I think I need say no more except to underline the unique position the CFL holds in Canadian sports.
The National Hockey League has had a majority of American teams for more than 50 years; so has the World Hockey Association since its inception two years ago. In other words, hockey got away from us a long time ago, before many of us were born. No strictly Canadian hockey league has been jeopardized by the operations of the NHL and WHA in Canadian cities. Baseball is also a very different story from football. The Montreal Expos play in the U.S. National League as major league baseball's only Canadian entry. There is not, and there never has been, a national Canadian professional baseball league to protect.

I heard the interjection by my friend, the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark). I am sure he knows there is not now a national Canadian professional lacrosse league in this country, and there has not been for quite a few decades.
However, in spite of the obvious lack of parallels between the situation of the Montreal Expos and the Toronto Northmen, it has been said, or at least whispered, that the government would not have acted to stop the Northmen if their franchise had been located in Montreal. At the risk of dignifying such allegations by replying to them at all, I can only repeat that the government's policy on the protection of Canadian football has been clearly stated and has been consistent since it was first announced in November, 1972: no foreign-based football leagues would be allowed to operate in Canada and there would be no exceptions to that rule. At the time that policy was stated, possible expansion of the NFL into Canada was centred not in Toronto but in Montreal.
It has also been suggested that the government acted to block the WFL only out of some devious and partisan political motives. As far as I know, both the old and the new Toronto Argonaut owners are prominent Conserva-
April 18, 1974

tives, so I cannot imagine what our alleged partisan political motives might have been. I am sorry to disappoint anyone, but our reasons for the legislation are not devious at all: they are as simple and straightforward as is our policy-to keep foreign football leagues out of Canada.

speechtext:
The Toronto Northmen consistently maintained that they were unaware of any federal government policy that would inhibit their operation until they received news reports of my speech in Regina on February 21 of this year. In that speech I reiterated the government's policy of November, 1972, and stated our determination to do everything possible to prevent the WFL from operating in Canada. All of the Northmen's arguments against the Canadian football bill and for excluding the WFL from some or all of its provisions are based on the flimsy premise that they did not know they were contravening government policy when they set themselves up in business. In other words, they have tried to convince people that they were simply unaware of government policy until February 21 and that they are, therefore, in fairness, entitled to special consideration.
For the benefit of the House, I am now going to review some facts that show the Northmen are in error when they say they did not know what government policy was. At a CFL executive meeting on November 16, 1972, Mr. John Bassett, Sr., representing the Toronto Argonauts football club, served notice that at the executive committee meeting on December 1 he would move a resolution providing that the Canadian Football League would approve the principle of the expansion of the league through the granting of new franchises which would be organized for the purpose of operating professional football clubs in the United States of America at such times as applications for such franchises were received by the league. Mr. Bassett also advised the November 16 meeting that he would move at the December 1 meeting that the commissioner be empowered to meet with Mr. R. Schmertz to negotiate the terms of application for a Canadian Football League franchise in New York city, such application to be submitted to the league for approval to be operative in the football season of 1976.
Following reports of the CFL meeting, the Hon. John Munro, then minister of national health and welfare, stated the government's view that any CFL expansion into the United States would represent an erosion of the indentity of Canadian football and the government would do everything possible to prevent it from happening. On November 21, 1972, Mr. Munro held a meeting in Ottawa to discuss the matter with Mr. Bassett and the CFL comm-missioner, Mr. Jake Gaudaur, and to find out why the CFL was contemplating expansion into the United States. The CFL representatives indicated that some CFL clubs were concerned that if the CFL did not expand into the United States, a new U.S.-based league would be formed that would grant franchises in Canada.
The minister advised Mr. Bassett and Mr. Gaudaur that it was government policy to oppose the expansion of the CFL into the United States as well as the expansion of any
Canadian Professional Football U.S. league into Canada. Mr. Bassett advised Mr. Munro that he would formally withdraw his notice of motion for CFL expansion into the United States at the next CFL executive committee meeting on December 1.
Mr. Munro made the federal government's position abundantly clear in a public statement on November 22, 1972. The story was carried by Canadian Press and was widely covered in the media. As a matter of fact, it was the subject of a front page story in the Montreal Gazette and the Toronto Star on the following day. Mr. Munro said that the government could apply sanctions to prevent expansion of the CFL south of the border into the United States, or expansion of U.S. leagues into Canada, or even formation of a new league with Canadian entries.
At the CFL executive committee meeting on December 1, 1972, Mr. Bassett formally withdrew his notice of motion concerning expansion into the United States. According to the minutes of the meeting, he also informed the committee about his meeting with Mr. Munro and stated that he had told the minister he did not intend to take any course of action contrary to declared government policy. So we know that Mr. Bassett, Sr., was fully aware of federal policy in November, 1972, when it was initially announced.
Now, what about Mr. John Bassett, Jr., president of the Toronto Northmen? At that time, Mr. Bassett, Jr., was a director of the Toronto Argonauts. His father was the president. The Bassetts are not only father and son; they are also business associates in several enterprises. They have other associates who share their interest in promoting. In addition, they are active in communications. It is therefore difficult to believe that Mr. Bassett, Jr., was completely unaware of federal policy when he acquired the WFL franchise.
On December 5, 1972, at a press conference as the newly appointed Minister of National Health and Welfare, I publicly stated my concurrence with the government policy Mr. Munro had announced. On December 11, 1972, I met in Ottawa with CFL president Bill Clarke and CFL commissioner Gaudaur and reaffirmed the government's position to them. On December 13, 1972, Mr. Gaudaur sent to all the CFL executive committee delegates and alternates- among whom were Messrs. John Bassett, Sr., and John Bassett, Jr.-a summary of his meeting with Bill Clarke and myself. In that summary he reported specifically that I, personally, and speaking for the federal government, continued to be concerned over the prospect of expansion of the CFL to the United States as well as the expansion of the NFL into Canada, and that in so far as the latter was concerned I would discuss with my colleagues what action might be taken by the government to deter or preclude NFL expansion into Canada.
On January 17, 1973, at a CFL executive committee meeting in Winnipeg, commissioner Gaudaur reported again on his December 11, 1972, meeting in Ottawa with Bil' Clarke and myself. The Toronto Argonauts representatives at the January 17, 1973, CFL meeting in Winnipeg were, according to the minutes, John Bassett, Sr., Lew Hayman and John Bassett, Jr.
In the light of all these facts, it is more than difficult to believe the Northmen's assertions that they were completely unaware of federal football policy until my speech on February 21, 1974.

This afternoon the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) suggested that we should go on to something else, that we should not spend much time on this particular issue as there were many others of importance facing this nation, certainly many of more importance than football. I agree with him, and we are ready to take up the offer of the official opposition in that respect. The bill is short and simple. There is no reason why we should not have a short debate and have this matter referred to committee for consideration, study and even the hearing of witnesses if the committee wishes.
I understand that discussions are being held with a view to concluding this debate tomorrow. I want to assure hon. members that we on this side of the House are more than willing to co-operate to that effect, either by limiting the number of speeches or by limiting the length of speeches. Our position is that we should make our decision and carry on with the business of the House. If there is any delay, it will not be blamed on this government.

I do not come from an area of Canada which has gained much from the protection of tariffs. We were sort of on the other side.
In common with many members here, I have over the years passed through many emotions on various debates. Sometimes one is amused, sometimes one is angry. Once in a while one is even informed. But tonight I am suffering from a sense of unreality. It almost passes my broadminded comprehension that, considering the state of this nation today, we in the House of Commons of Canada are dealing with a measure of this kind.

speechtext:
Inflation is soaring higher than the eagle-the American eagle, if I may be permitted to use that phrase because it is the highest flyer. Transportation, described by one of the chief authors of the transportation legislation as being in a mess one week ago, is still in a mess today. Many are here tonight listening to the minister's speech because of the curtailment of transportation. There is trouble on land, sea and in the air. We have gone beyond Paul Revere; he had only two media to contend with.
The country is rent with labour and industrial unrest. There is a housing crisis which is gripping and organizing the people of this country. We are not talking much about unemployment because it is becoming chronic and increasing and we are becoming used to it. We have a divided cabinet, with the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) saying one thing and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) another. We have a Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who comes back on the day the football bill is called.
Yet in the present state of the nation we are talking about what Mr. Bassett said to Mr. Schmertz, and whether there were two Bassetts at one meeting or one Bassett at two meetings. That is the kind of thing we are talking about here tonight. Some Herodotus could use this occasion to illustrate what Nero did. There are so many things that cry out for priority, cry out for attention, not only within the government but within the minister's own department.
I am, perhaps regrettably, not a sportsman but I respect those who find satisfaction in sport. Yet somehow I am somewhat concerned about the 25 per cent of Canadians who today are living on or below the poverty line. I am a little worried about what has happened to medical research funds in this country and the serious shrinkage of them. I am a little worried because no one on the government side seems to think that anything can be done about inflation. That is not too far removed from suggesting that nothing should be done about it. Yet in the midst of all this travail, in the midst of the anxiety of the Canadian people, we are counting football players. I say all this not to scorn the minister; I say it in all seriousness. While it is all very well to make fun of politicians, to make them the butt of the joke syndrome, things are serious when the institution itself is held up for public scorn and for resentment and questioning by the people whom it serves. That is why this is so serious. I do not feel happy, as a representative of the people of Canada, to think that this is the best thing we can find to do on this night.

speechtext:
I read the following in the Globe and Mail the other day:
Health minister Marc Lalonde says they shall not pass-and he is mustering every weapon in the democratic arsenal to blast the intruders from Canadian soil. Though confederation last 1,000 years, people will say that this was when it became a country fit for the Canadian Football League to play in.
It would be unsporting of us to go around quenching nationalist fires, and we understand perfectly that the federal government, having dealt adroitly and effectively with the problems of inflation, unemployment, poverty, the native peoples, immigration, energy, international relations, and health, must now accord priority to the fundamental issues of our day: which set of initials should be permitted to predominate on the football field.
As a greater man than I once said, "O temporal O mores!"
From Ottawa, Mr. Lalonde spotted a threatening manoeuvre developing in Toronto. A cheque book was seen to flutter in the breeze, and three Miami Dolphins football players were arrayed for the press as the latest acquisitions of the Toronto Northmen of the World Football League.
There were suggestions of a stiff diplomatic note, or sending for Henry Kissinger. This delightful editorial in the Globe and Mail ends:
Yet Mr. Lalonde's quivering finger continues to indicate an approaching peril, and on Parliament Hill they are pacing the battlements and checking their muskets. On guard for whom?
I am not much of a partisan; I spend most of my time supporting measures which this minister puts forward. He has received my support and commendation on many endeavours, many proposals and many legislative pieces, but tonight on this measure I am amazed. I wonder if this is the same person who from time to time has shown such lucidity and perception. Indeed, he is sometimes so progressive that he could find a place in our party.

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext: Since I quoted Cicero, I must be bilingual and refer to Shakespeare who wrote, "On what meat doth this our Caesar feed that he hath grown so great?"

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext: The pretensions and the parameters of this bill are, to say the least, startling. As I read the bill full of trembling, I read that people can go to jail for two years. My God, that is a non-sporting suggestion!

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext:
The preamble would do well as the prelude to the lyrical ballads of Wordsworth. I have read a lot of dry statutes and a lot of dull bills, but I have never read such a hyperbolic expression as this preamble. Indeed, I wonder where the preamble ends and the propaganda begins. What lawyer ever heard a "whereas" followed by this:
And whereas Canadian football developed for itself a unique national institution contributing to the strengthening of the bonds of nation-

April 18, 1974
Canadian Professional Football
hood and it is in the national and public interest that an effort be made to protect this institution from the encroachments of foreign sponsored enterprises extending into Canada;
Now, therefore, Her Majesty, by and with-
Mellow stuff that. We are today faced with this urgent and necessary matter, a matter of which we heard incidentally, or was it coincidentally, on April 10, 1974, the very day of the release of the March consumer price index which recorded the highest peacetime cost of living increase since the index was established. That was the day on which this measure was launched. What happy auspices! How it will delight the housewives of this nation to know that the two came together. The preamble of the bill is interesting. It reads:
Whereas football has an established tradition in Canada as witnessed by the cup symbolizing football supremacy in Canada, which was donated by His Excellency, the late Governor General Earl Grey in 1909 for that purpose-
In the definition section, the term "football" means:
-Canadian football and American football but does not include soccer or rugby-
There is something quite interesting here. It can be historically proven that the established tradition which sports football claims to hold with regard to the Grey Cup is basically untrue. When the Grey Cup was donated by Earl Grey in 1909, it was intended to symbolize Canadian supremacy in "rugby football".

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext:
Even a layman like myself can see that is a sport emphatically different from football as it is known today. Rugby, as pointed out in the definition of "football" for the purposes of this bill, is not to be considered in conjuction with the term "football". Even dear old Lord Grey, who was invoked so greatly by the minister, did not intend this sort of thing at all. Grey, of course, was not an outstanding Canadian. Some do not think he was an outstanding Englishman. But a Canadian he was not. He was not one who would ever earn legitimately a place in any pantheon of Canadian national football heroes. Certainly he would not be happy-God rest his imperial soul!-to know that things were distorted in such a way that that which he claimed to be the goals and the focus of his cup award is excluded by a bill which names him as a sort of remote, historic godfather.
I hope the minister does not think I am being critical of him or his bill. I want him to know that with the basic intention of preserving Canadianism in professional football we join in our support and in our applause. It would be highly unlikely, and quite out of historic proportion, if a spokesman for the party of Macdonald, Borden, Bennett and Diefenbaker was not in the forefront of sensible, strong nationalism. When it comes to asserting our nationalism, we take second place to no group, political or otherwise, in this country.

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext:
If hon. members do not believe me, they can ask some of the pals of Earl Grey who had to deal with Canadian nationals like Robert Borden. Or you might check with some of the American authorities who had to deal with the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. 
Diefenbaker) when he was prime minister, who when it came to the Trading with the Enemy Act did not engage in the protracted, pusillanimous patty-caking which went on in reference to WML-Worthington, but acted assertively and successfully.
We, of course, believe in sensible, sensitive nationalism in the whole spectrum of Canadian society. What we have to ask, as any thoughtful parliamentarian must ask, is whether the goal to which the minister alluded is likely to be reached by the measure before us. We have to inquire as to the likely efficacy of the measure, and we certainly have to examine its exclusive nature.
The minister has obviously decided to bring down a gridiron curtain on the forty-ninth parallel. What other protective measures does he envisage? Not being a sports fan, I do not understand all the subtleties, but it seems to me as a greenhorn, a layman, that though one sees baseball and other sports played in Canada by Canadian teams, there are always a lot of American players around. We know that in America there are great hockey teams, but even a greenhorn like myself recognizes that most of the players are Canadians. Bobby Orr is a great player, but Bobby Orr is not a true Bostonian. He is a Canadian. Does the minister intend to extend his sports nationalism to other areas, or is it football alone which deserves this special and unique legislative treatment-right up to two years in jail?
Canada's national game is not football. It is not hockey. It is lacrosse. Even since the minister's fearless Regina speech there have been two major exercises in what I would call the Americanization of lacrosse. But no one has murmured. No one has legislated or even threatened to legislate. What is wrong with lacrosse, our national game? Does it not deserve protection? Is it necessary to be both a footballer and a professional to be protected? Is that which is good for football, bad for lacrosse? Is our nationalism selective to the extent that it must be confined to football alone? My witty colleague from Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) put a question to the minister not long ago. He asked: "Does the minister plan to bring in legislation which would ensure that the Stanley Cup never leaves Canada?"

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext: Oh, Oh!

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext:
Lord Stanley was a Governor General. We are invoking Governors General now. Why doesn't he get a look in on this? These are hard questions for the layman to answer. But in realms other than professional sport one is troubled. Is there greater danger to the Canadian way of life from foreign football than from foreign forces in other fields? What of the arts? What of our universities? Many Canadian professors are expressing grave concern about the widespread appointment of American professors by American deans or American heads of departments in Canadian universities. If it is more dangerous to have "X" number of American football players out in the field than to have so many American professors in Canadian universities-many of them, incidentally, teaching Canadian studies-how do we measure this danger to our national soul?
April 18, 1974

When one reflects upon this question one gets into a realm approaching the ridiculous. Where will all this end? Where does it begin? And why does it begin? Are we really heading for a Fortress Canada where the full force of legislative power will decree what a citizen shall see, who shall play, who shall watch, who shall own, who shall coach, who shall form leagues? It is a horrendous prospect of prohibition. And I have never liked prohibition very much.

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext: From the very beginning I was troubled by the negative and restrictive aspect of the bill. I share with other Canadians a real appreciation of the CFL. I know what the Grey Cup means to so many of our people. If I were not a maritimer, I think I would like to be a westerner. I spent nine years of my life on the prairies and I learned a lot there. Indeed, as my former leader said, I was toughened up there when I was exposed and I understand exactly the feelings of some of those people toward certain aspect of this question. I know the Grey Cup means a great deal to a great number of our people, though I must say that as a maritimer I demur in the face of the contention that it symbolizes a national competition. As my hon. friend from Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) has often said, Canada does not begin at Montreal; there is an important area eastward-an area, in fact, where confederation first began. And I am proud, Mr. Speaker, to represent the very place where it began, the cradle of confederation, the city of Charlottetown.

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext: And I say in passing, without any rancour-and we maritimers are never rancorous-that football, or any other activity which does not include the Atlantic provinces, is something less than national. A moot question, of course, is whether the action this bill is intended to forestall would destroy, diminish or undermine the CFL. Mr. Speaker, when one does not know a subject it is always well to consult an expert. A great football player and also, in my opinion, a great educator is Mr. Russ Jackson of Ottawa.

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Jackson said, not long ago:
I just think that if the CFL is too weak to face this kind of competition, we are going to lose it eventually anyway. If it can't compete without government legislation, then some other league, some other team such as the Northmen, or some other sport entirely, will knock it out. I think Toronto is a strong enough football town to support both the Argonauts and the WFL.
Even if Mr. Jackson is wrong and I am wrong-not likely, I would think, in either case-and if the dangers are as great as pessimists paint them to be, were there no positive measures which could have been taken to sustain the CFL? Was there nothing else but a measure which, in my judgment, comes very close to being a bill of attainder directed against one individual?
The minister talks of his meetings with Mr. Bassett and Mr. Bassett's father. I have never seen Mr. Bassett in my
Canadian Professional Football life. The only millionaires that I know are those in the House here-and most of them are across the way. I would be about as much at home in the board room of big business as I would on the football field; and I would be just as comfortable on the flight deck of Mariner IV in that regard. But was it necessary to be so restrictive? Was it necessary to have, as I say, something approaching a bill of attainder, which I think the British knocked out about four centuries ago-it was practised in the pre-Stuart era. This friend of the minister's whom he met so often may be rich, but he was a Canadian, not a foreigner, and so far as I can make out he was not at the time breaking an existing law, which should give him a half decent chance to express himself in these matters.
There have been some interesting discussions on the sports pages about the ramifications of this measure. I have made a careful study of all this, Mr. Speaker. When one starts from zero one has to study very hard. I have noticed that many friends of the CFL are expressing doubt as to the capacity of this bill to assist that very important Canadian institution. Indeed, there are many who fear that the results will be inimical to the CFL itself. They point out some very impressive and cogent arguments.
After all, if the WFL does not go into Toronto, it will not disappear, or evaporate, or leave the face of the earth. It will still be there, this bill passed notwithstanding. It will still be around with its attraction or its pressure, whichever expression one wants to use. Because no matter what success the minister has with this bill, no matter what station he will attain, his fiat will not run below the forty-ninth parallel. There will still be functioning football groups there from which we will not be able to separate potential Canadian players, any more than we will be able to separate potential Canadian viewers. So the gridiron curtain will be penetrable in very important ways.
I suggest the minister might well reflect upon the serious problems facing this country and the exacerbation of economic difficulties which for many portions of the Canadian population are approaching the unbearable. I suggest he pause, reflect, and say to his colleagues, "I started out well, but things have so developed in more important areas of our economic society that I hope you agree with me that we should wisely move on to something that would help the mass of Canadian people" who have suffered so long from 11 years of callous maladministration.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am the member who is fortunate enough, I think- though you may feel otherwise-to lead off for our group on this bill. I want to say at the outset that my colleague, the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose), is the quarterback and chairman of our caucus committee having to do with areas such as sport, and had he been here tonight he would probably be leading off; and doing so, I know, better than I. The members of our caucus will be free to vote as they choose on this matter, but I expect and hope that most, if not all, will support the legislation.

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext:
I want to say that, unlike the hon. member who has just taken his seat, I am a football fan and I personally endorse and will support this legislation. The hon. gentleman, who was kind enough to close off his remarks to allow me to make mine this evening, which I appreciate very much, said that he was not a fan. My only reaction to that is that this is no time to brag about it. In fact, I am still not sure whether he is going to vote for or against this bill. However, if he is not a fan or a quarterback, he is a good water-boy, running about all over the economic and political spectrum and Canadian history, trying frantically to put out the fire over the Tory dilemma on whether or not to keep professional football in Canada, Canadian. The hon. member mentioned lacrosse, and I agree with him: I wish the minister had put a provision in this bill with regard to lacrosse and a number of other sports as well. But even the fact that the minister went this far is something.
Some will say that this is an area of endeavour in which the government of Canada has no business intruding.

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext:
I note some Saskatchewan Tories applauding that one, Mr. Speaker. That professional football is a private business and is of sufficient insignificance in terms of culture, the economy and Canadian content, as not to warrant legislation is the argument put forward by these people. I submit that it is important enough to warrant parliament's stepping in.
Professional sport, in this instance professional football, is not only a business but a large industry. Professional football in the last five years has reached very large proportions in terms of dollars and volume of public interest, television coverage and television fees, and it is in fact an industry-and a significant one-even though it involves sports.
The parliament of Canada on a number of occasions in the last several decades has seen fit to intervene and intrude when an industry of any kind threatens to do injury, in order to prevent that injury to some Canadian endeavour. I submit that in this instance professional

football is in the same category and I think it is proper for this parliament to intervene and intrude. When activities in professional football seem to be injurious or threaten the operation of our own professional sports industry, the government has an obligation to step in and prevent such a threat to at least that small part of our Canadian culture-and it is part of our Canadian culture.
In the past five years we have witnessed outstanding growth in professional sports both here and in the United States. Professional sport is no longer the preoccupation of a few sports-minded hobbyists. Coupled with our affluence, both gate and TV revenues from sport are extremely attractive to the diamond-studded aristocrats who can afford to buy sports franchises in major centres of the continent. There must be a number of these men in North America, because the expansion of league franchises, certainly in football and hockey, is enormous.
We are no longer dealing with a simple game, but a developing sports industry of major proportions. This major industry, I submit, should be subject to legislation and control just like any other business. It is a business. That is why I cannot accept the argument of those who say it is not the government's business whether the World Football League is allowed a Toronto franchise or whether the proposed $178 million stadium in Montreal, paid for by the people of Canada, will be used for an NFL franchise or for the Expos to play baseball in. A Montreal NFL franchise would be very attractive, of course, but not to the benefit of the people of Montreal and not to the benefit of Canadian football; it would be to the benefit of whichever mogul or covey of private entrepreneurs is successful in obtaining such a franchise.
In supporting the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) in his attempts to arrive at some solution to American athletic imperialism, many members of my party are extremely concerned about the future of the Canadian Football League and especially about the community-owned teams in western Canada. We are con-erned about the World Football League raiding the CFL for players, and that is why we back the minister in his stand against the WFL Toronto franchise application.
Anyone who would try to suggest that a World Football League franchise in Toronto will not harm the Canadian Football League is suffering delusions which must border on the delirium tremens that some people suffer. It is perfectly obvious that additional professional football teams in Montreal and Toronto could not help but reduce the gate receipts, television receipts and the receipts of the Argonauts in Toronto as well as the Canadian Football League, and anybody who suggests otherwise does not know what he is talking about. If Mr. Bassett wants to talk about a $48,000 gate equalization, I suggest he should make it $480,000 if he wants to talk sense. Such a franchise could not help but would hurt the Canadian Football League.
It is true that there are 15 Americans on each of the teams and most of the coaches and managers are American, but in spite of that there is a significant element of Canadian content, Canadian endeavour and Canadian effort and the majority of the players are Canadian. We also have Canadian rules, which in my personal opinion are a heck of a lot better than the rules of the National
April 18, 1974

Football League. The game is more exciting to watch, it is a better game, it is a faster game and it is our game.
I should also like to refer to community ownership of five of the Canadian Football League teams. Maybe there are some members of this chamber who are not concerned because they happen to come from Toronto, Montreal or Ottawa which do not have community-owned football teams; but in my province of Saskatchewan the Roughrid-ers team is ours, and the same applies to Winnipeg and the rest of Manitoba as well as to Edmonton, Calgary and Vancouver. Even those well-to-do and well-heeled Tories and Liberals who actively work for and support these teams are deserving of full marks and full credit because nobody makes a buck out of them. I hope the day will come when the people of Montreal, Toronto and Ottawa will take over and operate on a community basis professional football teams and teams in other sports as well.
Another reason I personally support the bill is that I am not particularly interested in the welfare of the millions of dollars of one, John Bassett, Jr. Let us not kid ourselves. I have sided with the minister's position on this because I see professional football as an industry in North America. Perhaps only three cities in Canada are capable of supporting big league professional football, that is, Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver; but if these three go American, you can kiss the other Canadian teams goodbye. And that is what the Bassett-Toronto deal means in the long run. Let us have no doubt about that.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Bassett has one very simple motive. He does not really care if he wrecks the Canadian Football League. He just wants to make himself a few more bucks.

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext:
My hon. friends to the right applaud that. I suggest that if Mr. Bassett wants to make a few more bucks out of football, he can damn well go to the United States and become an American citizen and make his bucks there, and leave our Canadian football alone. The Canadian Football League is not Canadian enough yet, and we all agree to that. The Canadian Football League must expand and must become even more Canadian. I would hope that within the next five or ten years the Canadian league is composed of even more, if not entirely, Canadian players.
We must also consider the efforts and the activities of our Canadian football teams in community and high school football leagues. The Saskatchewan Roughriders have provided equipment and professional assistance to a number of high school teams. For example, a great deal of such assistance was given to the high school football team in the little town of Maple Creek. We must consider the tens of thousands of dollars and the efforts that have been put into our high school, university and junior football teams. I do not hear Mr. Bassett offering any aid or comfort in that regard. He has put his money in his pocket and run. This is another good reason for having our own professional football league. It does something more than just try to make bucks for millionaires in Toronto, Buffalo, or somewhere else.
In addition to running the business of professional football, the CFL is also actively engaged in promoting ama-
Canadian Professional Football teur sports and in the development of Canadian talent on the part of players, coaches and managers. Surely that is another important part of the operation of the Canadian Football League and another reason for supporting the minister and the government on this bill.
I listened to the minister, followed by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie), talking about the old days long before I came here. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) might well have been here in those days. It is funny that mention was made of Sir John A. Macdonald and the national dream to keep the foreigners, the damned Yankees, out. Then there was R. B. Bennett, who in the late 1930s brought in the CBC and the Canadian Wheat Board. I am beginning to feel sorry I have been so critical of these historic figures of Canadian political life because it now looks as if they were a hell of a lot more progressive than the present Progressive Conservatives. I am not suggesting they were perfect. Mr. Macdonald's endeavours to get the construction of a transcontinental railway to knit together Canada was an excellent idea, but subsequently it turned out to be for the benefit of the CPR instead of for Canada. However, that can be corrected also. The NDP have some ideas on that.
I should like to urge hon. members to consider not only the community-owned teams of western Canada but also the other places in Canada that should be able to, and I hope will very soon, enter the Canadian Football League, such as London, Ontario, Halifax-Dartmouth and then, why not, Quebec city? I think British Columbia should have another team. Vancouver Island has the population to support a team. There is no way this can come about if we sit back and do not do anything just because a millionaire from Toronto wants to make a buck with an American franchise at the expense of some element at least of Canadian professional football league operations in this country. If that is nationalism, good. I think it is a lot better kind of nationalism than the hon. member for Hillsborough has put forward. He spoke about sensitive and sensible nationalism. That is fine. He wondered what other method might have been found to protect the Canadian Football League. I wish he would quit wondering and tell us what his ideas are and what the Conservative Party would do, if anything.
I hope the hon. members for Regina East (Mr. Balfour), Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Horner) and Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton) will speak, because I should like to hear their views. I am sure the people in their constituencies who buy season tickets to support the Saskatchewan Roughriders would like to hear their views. In fact, I am sure the busload or two of people who make the 300 mile round trip to the home games in Regina from Swift Current would be very interested to hear what the hon. member from that constituency would say and how he would vote on this bill.
I hope the hon. member for Regina East lets us know where he stands on this. In case he or any other such members are unable to be present for the vote, I hope they will tell us where they stand on this question because I am sure the people from the steel plants, the packing houses and the railway yards in Regina, as well as the downtown storekeepers-the people who pool their money to buy

April 18, 1974
Canadian Professional Football tickets to the $100 dinner, and season tickets-will be interested to hear what the hon. member has to say. But more importantly they will be interested to know where he stands.
I agree with the hon. member for Hillsborough that this legislation is not as important an issue as inflation, or the corporate tax rip-off, the railways or what is being done by the government in the wrecking of the Canadian Wheat Board with the support of the Conservative Party. However, this matter is important and I want to ask my friends in the Progressive Conservative Party or anyone in my party who does not support this bill, for God's sake can't we have something of our own, or must we lose it because some millionaire wants to buy a football franchise? Is it not time to say, "No, no further"?
Of course this is not as important as many other serious issues facing this country, but I submit it is important enough for this parliament to deal with and it is important enough for this parliament to do something about. We need not take a long time tomorrow dealing with this bill at the second reading stage. If the hon. member for Hillsborough wishes to get on with something more important, I hope he will persuade his colleagues to take two minutes each tomorrow, then sit down and we will have a vote next week. Next Monday we could start dealing with something more important than professional football: we would spend merely a minimum of time in the House on this measure.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to urge upon members that it is important enough for them to even change their minds and support the legislation. It is important enough that the passage of this kind of legislation will serve notice and warning on people of the ilk of the Bassetts in other sports in other parts of the country. It is important enough that I think the government then might be encouraged to do more about other sports of a professional and semi-professional nature in this country. I wish to urge, certainly on my behalf, and I think on behalf of most if not all my colleagues, that this legislation is worth supporting and that if the Canadian Football League is worthy of extending and expanding I hope all of us will decide it is worth passing this bill, because we do not have too much time.
