subtopic: AIR CANADA-NEGOTIATIONS RESPECTING USE OF WINNIPEG AS OVERHAUL BASE FOR BOEING 727 AIRCRAFT
AIR CANADA-NEGOTIATIONS RESPECTING USE OF WINNIPEG AS OVERHAUL BASE FOR BOEING 727 AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the past year I have risen many times to speak on subjects relating to Air Canada. As everyone who has ever flown on Air Canada knows, there is a great deal wrong with our national airline. Specifically, my interest in Air Canada centres around the transfer of the air maintenance base from Winnipeg to Dorval in 1969 and the concomitant problems which have ensued both in Winnipeg and Dorval. Hon. members are only too familiar with the history surrounding the move, so I will not
April 18, 1974

expand on it again except to say that the transfer effectively destroyed Manitoba's aerospace industry. It was thus heartening to hear that the government may finally be doing something to revive the industry. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) is to be congratulated for his stand to establish an Air Canada overhaul base in Winnipeg.
Since the departure of the base, the Manitoba aviation industry has floundered as successive Liberal governments have failed to honour their commitments to that industry. Air Canada's successor at the Winnipeg base, CAE Aircraft, has been beset with difficulties ever since it took over the operation. Government contracts or assistance have not been forthcoming as promised, and as a result the aerospace industry in Manitoba is slowly dying. But this is no real surprise. After all, CAE could never hope to replace Air Canada.
What is needed in Winnipeg is not government and Air Canada contracts to CAE but the return of portions of the Air Canada overhaul base from Dorval to Winnipeg. This would allow many of the 1,000 or so Manitobans who were drafted to Dorval to return home, and it would allow former Air Canada employees who are now with CAE to return to Air Canada at a higher rate of pay. It would also rebuild what was once a viable industry in the province and provide the government with an opportunity to live up to its avowed policy of industrial decentralization. To date this policy has been an outright sham, especially with regard to Air Canada. The government seems to forget that a confidential transportation study completed in 1971, the McKinley report, recommended that Air Canada's operations be decentralized.
Both the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) have said that the government is firmly committed to a policy of industrial decentralization within Canada and have talked at great length of the need to develop secondary industry in the west on top of our great resource and energy base. Well, here is their chance to put their money where their mouths are. The McKinley report was correct in recommending that Air Canada decentralize its operations. After all, Air Canada operated two bases for several years and did so very efficiently. Just look at the 1957 Wallace Clark report. Furthermore, most American airlines operate their maintenance and overhaul of both aircraft and engines on the fleet base station concept. That respected periodical, the Journal of Air Law and Commerce, listed the following advantages of decentralization: shorter lines of authority, greater field economics, and increased stress on the profit centre concept and cost control.
The problems at Dorval to which I alluded earlier have been the subject of many of my previous remarks regarding Air Canada. Suffice it to say that these relate to safety, staffing and the violation of various regulations-all problems which the unions have brought to the attention of Air Canada management. While nothing has been done to alleviate these problems, Air Canada apparently has finally realized they exist: witness the recent replacement of the vice-president in charge of maintenance.
As well, Dorval is overcrowded and operating close to maximum efficiency. The result of such a situation is increased inefficiency. Currently, Wardair, Air Jamaica,
Adjournment Debate
Easter Airlines, Quebec Air and CP Air all make use of the Dorval facilities along with Air Canada. Any union fears that a transfer of parts of the maintenance base to Winnipeg would result in a loss of jobs are unfounded. Air Canada operations are increasing at the rate of 10 per cent annually, and thus there would be no shortage of work. Also, the airlines I have mentioned no doubt will be adding to their fleet, which will continue to create a high level of work for the Dorval air base.
In view of this entire situation it was thus heartening, as I mentioned, to hear that there have been consultations over getting Air Canada to assign some of its jet overhaul activities from Montreal to the Winnipeg base, and over the defence department's related plans to have the repair and overhaul of their Boeing 707s done in Winnipeg as well. Because the overhaul of the 707s is related to the establishment of further repair and overhaul work in Winnipeg, it is to be hoped that the government and Air Canada will decide to send Air Canada's Boeing 727s to Winnipeg instead of Montreal. And this does not mean assigning the work to CAE. Rather, portions of the base must be moved from Dorval to Winnipeg.

speakeroldname: Mr. Leonard Hopkins (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: AIR CANADA-NEGOTIATIONS RESPECTING USE OF WINNIPEG AS OVERHAUL BASE FOR BOEING 727 AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since Air Canada has ordered Boeing 727 aircraft, the first of which are due for delivery this fall, it had to make arrangements for their maintenance. At first, these aircraft will be providing an improved Rapidair service between Montreal and Toronto, and it therefore makes sense that such aircraft be maintained, initially, at Dorval. In due course, as more and more aircraft of this type are delivered and as the entire Air Canada fleet is increased in response to the growth in demand, Air Canada will no doubt assess the optimal way of arranging maintenance for its aircraft in an efficient manner.
As the hon. member knows, the corporation's management is responsible for the performance of the airline. Naturally, it is of interest to the government to know how the airline, as a Crown corporation, is harmonizing its corporate objectives in providing safe and efficient transportation to Canadians, with other government policies, without jeopardizing the viability of its main activity. As you are very well aware, the government is involved in a very comprehensive review of Canada's aerospace industry, and the contribution that Canadian airlines can make in this, especially Air Canada, is not overlooked. Air Canada's participation in the development of such strategies cannot be based on any one particular aircraft type but, rather, on its wider need for the maintenance of its fleet.

subtopic: HOUSING-ACTION BY GOVERNMENT TO REDUCE COST
HOUSING-ACTION BY GOVERNMENT TO REDUCE COST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reason I am speaking tonight before this "packed" House is that on April 10 I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) specifically what measures

April 18, 1974
Adjournment Debate
the government had in mind to deal with the rising costs of housing and whether he was able to give an assurance to the Canadian people and to parliament that the cost of housing, which has risen at a staggering rate within the last year, could be slowed down. The minister, of course, did not answer my question. He replied by saying:
Mr. Speaker, we cannot give the hon. member that guarantee, but we can assure him that we share his view of the seriousness of the problem he has stated.
That is some consolation for a person who cannot afford a house! In a previous answer the minister explained the reason why housing had jumped at such a remarkable rate when he said:
Basically, one of the problems is the excessive demand for housing within the middle income group which is produced, first, by an attempt by Canadians to protect themselves against inflation and, second, because the profit from the disposal of a house is still the only thing free of capital gains tax.
In other words, because of this incompetent government, people are forced to invest in housing and that is part of the reason for the cost of housing going even higher. Figures were released just recently which show that the cost of the average house in Toronto jumped within the last year by 41.8 per cent. The average house in Toronto at the present time is selling for about $50,435. Throughout Ontario in 1973, the increase in housing costs was 26.2 per cent. In my community houses have virtually doubled in price since 1970.
A study recently done in Ottawa before the latest increase in the mortgage rate showed that the average family which wanted to buy the average house here needed an income of $17,000 a year to pay for the mortgage, roughly two-thirds more than the average family makes at present. The problem is not quite so bad if you own your own house and plan to move to another, because the price of your own house will have appreciated along with the market. What is particularly bad is the prospect that literally millions of young Canadians, like myself, may never in their lifetime afford adequate housing of their own.
What is particularly shocking is the most recent hike in interest rates which has taken place since the time I asked my question of the minister. Our party has asked the government to bring in a series of comprehensive controls. The government has refused. We asked them to remove the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials which in itself is inflationary and helps the government to profit from the cost of inflation the average consumer must bear. Again they refused. We asked the government to bring in an early budget. Again they refused. Obviously, part of the government's so-called anti-inflation program is the latest increase in the bank rate. The effect on housing will not be to repress prices but, rather, to drive them up more. The government's actions, ostensibly to curb inflation, only make it worse. Yesterday's Toronto Star says:
"People are determined to buy houses now because they feel prices are going to keep on rising," one trust company official said.
Another said dearer mortgages will scare off only a few potential buyers who previously could barely scrape up the financing.

It is worth reading into the record part of the lead editorial in tonight's Toronto Star. It is entitled "Interest rates feed inflation" and reads in part:
In the case of businesses, interest payments are another cost item, just like labour and materials. When the price of any of these goes up, businesses pass the added cost along in the form of higher prices for their products.
By way of illustration, a spokesman for Trans Canada PipeLines Ltd. was quoted this week as saying his company "is not directly concerned" with higher wellhead prices for natural gas as long as it can pass the increases along in full to the ultimate users.
As for those ultimate users, many have no such quick and easy way of covering their higher costs. They have little economic muscle and can only watch helplessly as their pay cheques spread thinner month by month. So the burden of fighting inflation falls on their backs.
That's why, with inflation running at an annual rate in excess of 10 per cent, a further cost increase in the form of higher interest rates is not only inappropriate, but intolerable.
The government claims that inflation is largely imported. Of course, statistics show that two-thirds of our inflation is generated domestically. I think the people of Canada are entitled to more than a government which refuses to act. They are entitled to the option of choosing a new government if they so wish-and the polls show they are prepared to do that. That is why the government has refused to call an opposition day, when a vote of non confidence could be moved, before the budget. They are afraid of facing the electorate. The government is in decay, leaderless. Before today, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was down south, it was literally leaderless. Further, it is visionless. It stumbles from crisis to crisis. I and my party think that the Canadian people deserve something better.

speakeroldname: Mr. J.-Roland Comtois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: HOUSING-ACTION BY GOVERNMENT TO REDUCE COST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would answer very briefly to the comments of the hon. member for Welling-ton-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo (Mr. Beatty) to remind him that there has been much activity in the residential building industry in recent years. Costs of residential houses and apartment rents have risen significantly during the same period, partly because of ever higher wages and costs of building materials and serviced lots, partly because of the continuing strong demand for housing resulting from the desire for better accommodation and from inflation obsession.
Several initiatives have been taken by the federal government. To reduce the cost of serviced lots, for example, the government allocated from the budget of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, $100 million yearly for five years, to its land servicing program. This loan reserve is available to provinces and municipalities wishing to buy and service residential lots. The government provided also a significant amount, $135 million, for sewage treatment under the loan program. Under this program, municipalities may borrow an amount equal to two thirds of the cost of sewage disposal plants and main ducts construction. The municipalities can benefit from a subsidy equal to 25 per cent of the loan granted.
Further to these measures which have been passed to help provinces and municipalities turning lots into residential districts, hon. members will recall the changes to the National Housing Act which were passed last year and
April 18, 1974

especially the program to help low income homeowners to borrow from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at preferred rates. Under the program to facilitate the purchase of a house for low income families, they can borrow at a very low interest rate, as low as 6 per cent.
To summarize, Mr. Speaker, in 1974 the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will allocate the major part of its budget to housing programs for low and middle income people and to programs to help provinces and municipalities in the development of residential lots. Furthermore, the hon. members will remember the passing of Bill C-135, a few months ago, which has allowed us to increase funds available for housing.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-ELIGIBILITY FOR BENEFITS OF UNEMPLOYED RURAL WORKERS
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-ELIGIBILITY FOR BENEFITS OF UNEMPLOYED RURAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier today I directed a question to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) regarding the Unemployment Insurance Act which I feel discriminates against people in rural Canada. I base this on the interpretation that is made of the act by the officials, referees and umpires as to whether a person is actually available for work or whether he is restricting himself in terms of the distance from home he will go when trying to obtain a job. Because of the strict interpretation of these regulations, I also asked whether the Unemployment Insurance Commission expected a family to uproot itself in order to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits.
The minister replied that all I have to do is give him the information, he will look into the case and all will be well. The fact is, I have done that on numerous occasions. Almost every member from rural Canada has done the same. This is something that cuts across party lines. I have been told by members of the Conservative Party, the Liberal Party and my party from five or six provinces that they have run into the same problem where people in rural areas clearly qualify for unemployment insurance but because they live in a small town and cannot travel 40 or 50 miles-

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-ELIGIBILITY FOR BENEFITS OF UNEMPLOYED RURAL WORKERS
speechtext: Many do not have cars.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-ELIGIBILITY FOR BENEFITS OF UNEMPLOYED RURAL WORKERS
speechtext:
As the hon. member has pointed out, many do not have cars. They do not have adequate transportation. They are not in the same position to look for a job as people in urban Canada. The act is very subjective. It leaves it open to interpretation when deciding whether someone is available for work. For example, there is no mileage qualification which indicates a person must look for employment within 10, 20 or 40 miles. As a result, many people in rural Canada are discriminated against. I say this for two reasons. First, as all members know, job opportunities in rural Canada are scarce. Second, many of these people do not have cars and public transportation is not available to them in order that they may travel 40 or 50 miles to find a job.
There are many cases of this in my constituency. There is a woman, a farm wife, in the town of Balcarres, 55 miles from Regina, who had worked for many years. She became
Adjournment Debate
unemployed for very legitimate reasons. She applied for unemployment insurance. She made it very plain to the commission that she would work in her own town or in another town adjacent to her own town, and that she was willing to work at jobs which were much lower in pay, status, and so on, than she was qualified for. But the Unemployment Insurance Commission said she had to look for a job in the city of Regina. That is 55 miles away. She has no car-her husband needs the family car for his business. Therefore she was disqualified. If she had uprooted her family and moved into Regina, she could have qualified. It seems to me that this is a rather ludicrous thing to happen.
The other thing which I often find, Mr. Speaker, is that if a person were actually to lie to the Unemployment Insurance Commission and say, "I'll look for a job anywhere at any salary", then they would qualify; but if they are honest with the Unemployment Insurance Commission, they are cut off. I have in my hand a file with maybe 10, 15 or 25 cases at least in the last few months where precisely this has happened. People who move from a rural area into an urban centre and look for a job but can't find a job right away are cut off because they are restricting themselves. I have here a ruling of an umpire. This is back in June of 1973.1 quote the ruling regarding this particular point:
The umpire, who is the final authority for interpreting the Unemployment Insurance Act, has established the following principles when considering questions of availability for work:
1.	A person who leaves employment in an industrial area to take up residence in a small town or rural area fails to prove that she is available for work.
2.	A person who restricts herself to employment in a small town where opportunities for employment are limited, fails to prove that she is available for work.
I know people who have been willing to go 40 or 50 miles, to pay babysitters, to drive their own cars 40 and 50 miles, but the UIC people say these persons are not available for work. For God's sake, if a person lived in one of the cities of urban Canada and took exactly the same attitude, that person would qualify for UIC. A person in my riding, or in a comparable rural riding is not abusing the act; he is just desirous of getting the same benefits from the Unemployment Insurance Act as someone who happens to live in urban Canada.
What I am saying tonight to the parliamentary secretary and to the government is that they should do one of two things. They should either change the directive so as to enable the officials to interpret the act in a different way, or they should amend the act so that rural people would not be discriminated against by reason of the facts of geography; so that rural people do not have to connive or try to deceive the Unemployment Insurance Commission officials. I telephoned the Unemployment Insurance office in Regina today to find out how many claimants have been disqualified for the reason I have mentioned. Apparently this statistic is not kept. I suggest that it should be kept. In rural southern Saskatchewan, the area from which I come, several people were disqualified after having first qualified for UIC, and I suspect that most of them were disqualified for this reason.

April 18, 1974
Adjournment Debate
My last point is this. I believe women are discriminated against more than men under this particular provision. This is for various reasons. The husband may be employed in a rural area and the wife is looking for a job. The officials seem to interpret the act very religiously and very tightly. I could go on at great length and recite many cases. The minister knows all about this situation. I have been in touch with him several times. Members of all parties have been in touch with him. All I am saying is that some action should be taken to clarify this situation because at present there is discrimination against people who live in rural Canada whether they come from one province or another.

speakeroldname: Mr. Mark MacGuigan (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-ELIGIBILITY FOR BENEFITS OF UNEMPLOYED RURAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not the policy of the UIC to disqualify rural workers from benefit on the pretext that they are restricting their area of employment search. On the contrary, the commission simply requires, in accordance with the act, that claimants, whether urban or rural, prove that they are unable to obtain suitable employment in order to be eligible for regular benefits. The manner in which this proof is requested by the commission is through the job search statement which the claimant completes as he looks for re-employment. This listing of potential employers contacted provides the basis for continuing eligibility for benefits.
The one difference between the magnitude and the area of search required between urban and rural claimants is the distance from their residence that they should search for work. Rural claimants characteristically work within a range of some 25 to 30 miles from their residence. In fact, it is likely that they obtained their insurable employment with employers that far from home. It is therefore reasonable to require that they should search for work within that same reasonable distance. Urban claimants, on the other hand, do not normally work at such distances from their residence and in fact can usually make sufficient contacts with prospective employers within much shorter distances.
It is important to note that any denial of benefits, whether to urban or rural claimants, can be appealed by the claimant to a board of referees. This board of referees is generally composed of independent people selected from the claimant's community who have a knowledge of the work patterns of the claimants appealing. In point of fact, the insurance agent who makes the initial decision on a claim is also knowledgeable about a claimant's area and the distances which people in his district would normally travel to and from work.
Once a claimant has proved that he or she is unable to obtain suitable employment, the commission is obliged to continue to pay benefits. There is no requirement for claimants to move from their residence in order to obtain unemployment insurance benefits. If the claimant obtains his insurable employment in the area of his residence, then he or she is entitled to receive benefits while residing in that area provided be on she adequately show that they are unable to obtain employment.
The question that the hon. member has raised tonight is difficult to discuss because essentially it is a question of fact. But what strikes me very much about it is that the decision on this question of fact is made by officials who live in the area and it is reviewed by a board of referees who live in the area. It is hard to imagine people who could more adequately decide the facts in cases of this kind. We would be most happy to review any cases the hon. member cares to submit to the minister for review.
